https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr89: Video of the strikes on Russian ships was shared by Ukraine's President Zelensky
A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones at a port in Libya on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

There was an explosion on the warship at the Benghazi naval base in the early morning, while it was docking for fuel and supplies ahead of its return to Russia, the government that controls eastern Libya said.
Zelensky added that Ukraine's attack hit a second Russian vessel, a cargo ship which he claimed was being used to transport weapons.

The health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast of the port. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.
Following the strikes, Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region", but declined to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.
In a statement on Monday, Zelensky praised an "exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia's war".
Seven naval drones were deployed to target and sink the corvette Merkury, one of Russia's newest ships, Zelensky wrote. He added that a Ka-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed.
The Ukrainian president said the second ship was the MV ANGARA, a Russian container carrier.

The attack came the day after a Russian cargo vessel was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland . The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning.
Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has not commented.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday that the "expansion of terrorist activity in the Baltic" was a "dangerous trend" and said "it is, of course, leading to an escalation of tensions in the region."
When questioned over the attacks in Libya, Peskov said information would be provided by the country's defence ministry and added: "We paid attention to Zelensky's statements about it".
declined to comment on the strikes on Russian ships in Libya and said that that information would be provided by Russia's Defence Ministry.
The UN mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the attacks on Sunday, calling for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation".
"Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts," the UNSMIL wrote on X. , external

Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.

US-based intelligence firm Vantor collected high-resolution images that it said showed Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette (Merkury) - a Russian navy ship - moored in the port on Saturday, and on Sunday showed most of the same ship capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible.

The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.

GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.

Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqwy: Australia's Chris Bowen sits at the top table at the summit surrounded by other delegates
Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.
Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.
But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.
Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.
The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".

He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose country co-hosted the talks, attributed the failure to "difficult geopolitical times".
After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday to try to break the deadlock.

But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023 , when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.

The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".
"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.
Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.
A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.
Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions.
Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".
Climate advocates reacted with dismay at the failure of the talks.
Former US vice-president and climate advocate Al Gore said it was "outrageous that a handful of petro-states have veto power over any mention of fossil fuels".
The COP process was "in need of significant reform", Gore wrote on X, as most countries sought "to move forward in good faith."
"It's time that we empower those leaders with a reinvigorated multilateral process that reflects the latest science and represents the will of the majority of the world," he added.
Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts.
Last year at COP30 in Brazil , nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.
But this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8r4: The UN estimates that Israeli forces dropped more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives on Gaza in almost two years (file photo)

Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the non-profit organisation Oxfam says , external .

Heavy metals, explosive residues, and asbestos from destroyed buildings, dioxins and biological contaminants in the air, soil and water supply are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.
Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, accuses Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza."
"The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival," he says.
Israel's government has been asked for its response to the report.

It has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. Israel maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.
The report says 99% of Gaza shows indicators of potential environmental contamination

Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.

The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".

Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.
"There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.
She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.
Only a small fraction of the more than 60 million tonnes of debris in Gaza has been cleared

With all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.

Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.
UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.

The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqdr: 'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes hit Kyiv

A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer, in the Kyiv region, after 14 hours. Overnight Russian strikes on the village killed 11 people, Ukrainian officials have said.
The attack occurred in the early hours of Sunday. A 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive from the collapsed building, Kyiv's regional head Tymur Tkachenko said.
A strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 wounded in a separate strike on Vyshneve, also in the Kyiv region, that hit a grocery store on Sunday.
Ukrainian authorities said the boy in Dymer is in stable condition and was taken to hospital, and have thanked everyone involved in saving his life.
Zelensky and Ukraine's national police also confirmed the rescue of the boy.
In a Telegram post, Tkachenko said the 79-year-old woman rescued from the rubble was receiving treatment in hospital.
Earlier he said six people were injured in the attack, while others were still missing.
The attack on the residential building occurred in the early hours of the morning while people were asleep
Zelensky said more than 130 people are involved in emergency operations at the scene, and that they will continue until they have "complete information about every single person".
Sending his condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed, he said the strike struck the residential building, "practically blowing a section of it to smithereens".
Zelensky added that "rescue efforts are complicated by constant new air raid alerts and renewed threats".
The strike hit the building at 05:00 local time, when families were still asleep, Ukraine's minister of internal affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi said.
More than 70 strikes have been launched across 10 Ukrainian regions as of Sunday evening, Vyhivskyi added.
Emergency workers continue to search for those missing after Russian drone and missile attacks in Dymer.
In his video address posted online, Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 injured in a strike on an "ordinary grocery store" in Vyshneve.
Mayor Illya Dikov wrote on social media that three children were among the injured.
Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukraine's Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said in a post on X. , external

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwdr: Brussels Airport is receiving no travellers until 21:00 on Monday
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and train services have been severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted in Zaventem airport in the capital, Brussels, as well as Charlerois, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
Trains and underground services have also been halted in Brussels where large numbers of people are expected to join a protest march.

The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever has so far failed to agree a budget to cut costs with his coalition allies. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.

No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers. More than 50,000 travellers' plans were being disrupted - with more expected to be affected overnight and on Tuesday.
A similar situation has affected Charlerois, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure of arrival.
"Without air traffic control, no flights can take off or land," the airport said on Saturday when the strike action was announced, warning of "disastrous consequences".
As thousands descended on Brussels for the protest march, the leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".
"A genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes," Bert Engelaar, head of FGBT, said.

"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," Engelaar said, praising the left-wing Vooruit party - the only member of the five-party governing coalition reported to have stalled efforts to agree the budget.
Vooruit wants to raise taxes on the rich, and fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.
Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.
Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.

Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu says the presidential villa suffers from cuts in electricity and water - failures that plague ordinary citizens.
He said he was shaving last week when the water supply at the villa, known as Aso Rock, in Abuja cut.
He is seeking re-election next January and vowed to address these issues..
Tinubu made the disclosure on Sunday at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family in Lagos.
He explained: "On the Wednesday of last week, I was shaving, and the water went off. In the villa, you won't know punishment dey dia too [there’s punishment there too in Nigerian pidgin].
"The water went off. So we will correct all this. No light, no water, no electricity, no development. We have just started. We can do it, and we will do it for Nigeria,” he said.
Aso Villa serves as both the office and official residence of the Nigerian president. It is situated at the base of Aso Rock in Abuja.
Many Nigerians rely on generators like these to power their homes and businesses

Nigeria has long endured electricity shortages, but recent severe disruptions have been caused primarily by insufficient gas supplies and declining hydropower output, rather than the usual nationwide grid collapse.
Persistent blackouts in Lagos, Abuja and elsewhere have forced distribution companies to implement rotating power cuts, severely impacting households and businesses.
The country also suffers from chronic water shortages, the result of a structural crisis rooted in the gap between rapid urban population growth and decaying, inadequate public water infrastructure.
Tinubu made a high-profile electricity promise during the 2023 election campaign, but the exact wording and how binding it is has become a major point of contention ahead of the 16 January election.
Tinubu defeated the country’s former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar as well as Peter Obi in 2023 and the three are seen as the strongest contenders once again.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmvg: The meeting between Kenya's President William Ruto (left) and DR Congo's Félix Tshisekedi (centre) was hosted by Denis Sassou Nguesso (right)

Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
Relations between the two countries have soured since 2023 when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting leaders launching a rebel alliance, including the M23.
This led DR Congo to recall its envoy to Nairobi. Relations deteriorated further when Kinshasa refusing to accredit Kenya's nominated ambassador.
On Sunday, the two leaders affirmed their commitment to "sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of states".

The agreement was announced in a joint statement issued after the summit held in the town of Oyo in Congo-Brazzaville, facilitated by the nation's President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togolese leader Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé as mediator.
Tshisekedi and Ruto also agreed to "good neighbourliness and peaceful settlement of disputes" as well as "strengthen cooperation within regional mechanisms".
DR Congo and Kenya are both members of the East African Community (EAC).

DR Congo, which joined in 2022, is the latest entrant to the bloc, but its membership has been complicated by its accusation that Rwanda, a fellow member, backs the M23 rebels. Rwanda denies the claims despite overwhelming evidence.
DR Congo has also accused Kenya of hosting Congolese political and rebel leaders whom it says are working to destabilise the country.
When the Congo River Alliance (AFC), a political-military alliance including the M23, was launched in Nairobi in 2023, DR Congo responded by recalling its ambassador to Kenya.

The tensions were stoked further in March last year after Kenya named a consul-general to Goma, the capital of DR Congo's North Kivu region, after it fell to M23 forces, who control many eastern parts of the country.
DR Congo said naming the envoy amounted to disrespect for the country's territorial integrity and seemed to legitimise the group's occupation.
Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader
Relations deteriorated further after Kenya hosted a meeting of Congolese opposition figures, including former President Joseph Kabila , in October 2025.
Kabila was in 2025 sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself.
He has since been named the leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), the new rebel coalition that took over from the AFC.
Sunday's meeting between Ruto and Tshisekedi also included other issues including deepening trade cooperation, economic development, and regional integration.
The two also sought to collaborate to control the spread of the Ebola virus.

On Sunday, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said the frequency of attacks across the country's east had increased since the end of October, seriously affecting the Ebola response.
Tedros said heavy fighting in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged had disrupted work and the wider Ebola response.
More than 5,700 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.
The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, has spread beyond DR Congo borders, with cases reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj75: Finland says work is continuing on the Sparta II ship on Sunday
A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.
The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.
It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.
The Sparta II was "slightly listing", Finnish authorities added, but the "situation is stable" and no fuel or other "hazardous substance leaks" had been detected.
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

While Besprozvannykh initially said the crew of the Sparta II intended to repair the ship and carry on their journey, the Finnish Border Guard later said they had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was en route to Russia.
Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of maritime operations at the Finnish Border Guard, said during a news conference on Sunday that one Sparta II crew member had suffered minor injuries.
The Russian rescue vessel Murman is leading towing operations with the support of a Finnish guard ship and a Estonian naval patrol vessel.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Border Guard was responsible for the investigation into the attack and was co-operating with other relevant authorities.

The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland .

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw3d: How South Korea tackles cheating on its college entrance exam
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.
He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.

A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.
The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.
South Korean high school pupils in Daegu check their answers, a day after the annual college entrance exam
"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.
"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.
The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.
Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.
This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.
This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.

Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.
The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.
It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.
Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.
Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.
Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6vg: Watch: Democrat who unseated 21-year Republican incumbent says party needs to 'bring change'
The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.
The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.
The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.
Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.

Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.

"I think the American people are just sick of what's going on and they wanted a change. They voted for change," Hubbard told the BBC News Channel after his victory. He pledged to work alongside his fellow lawmakers to hold President Donald Trump accountable.
Earlier, he wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".

Hubbard added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."

Foxx, meanwhile, said in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."
Virginia Foxx spent a decade in the North Carolina Senate before representing the state in the House of Representatives

Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.
Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters.
Trump himself - as well as Vice President JD Vance - have suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses.
Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.

The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes.

Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law.
However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgl: The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filing shows.

"To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."
The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.
The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The army now plans to act by 24 November under an emergency exemption.

In the new filing, the Department of the Army argued that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion, a risk it said would become more likely as temperatures were set to fall in the coming days.

"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states.
It argued that the army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored in preparation for the detonation and that made the explosives more "vulnerable to temperature changes".
The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.

Earlier, the army had warned residents to leave their homes for six hours on the original scheduled day of the explosion, for the duration of the explosion and until the dust settled. An advisory warned "all humans" to avoid being outside in the affected areas while the demolition detonation was set to take place.

Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the IAAAP found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.
On Friday, the military said it was working with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the explosion was done in the safest manner possible.
Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place was the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.

The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".

One of the Environmental groups suing to pause the detonation, the Iowa Environmental Council, argued that many Iowans living within the risk-zone were unaware that the explosion was scheduled to happen.
"There is no safe level of lead exposure, and Iowans were given just days to prepare for the November 20 detonation," the organisation said in a press statement.
The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, which filed the lawsuit on Thursday that prompted the court-ordered pause, filed a new motion on Sunday in response to the army's filing.
The group asks the court to pause proceedings so that it may submit additional information before the scheduled detonation.

The motion includes declarations from environmental experts and local officials who support pausing the detonation, citing a lack of public notice and questioning the Army's claim that delay would cause significant risks.

At least three people have been killed after a fire at a confectionery factory in western Java on Saturday, with the death toll expected to rise.
Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for around 36 missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.
Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.
Rescuers recovered 24 body bags from the fire as of Sunday evening, as search operations continue to locate missing people.
Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire on Saturday evening.
The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km (31km) west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.

Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.
Local media reported that the search had been called off for the night late on Sunday, and would resume on Monday.
"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.
Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP.

Firefighters had been called to the building at 16:30 local time (09:30 GMT) on Saturday - but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz.
"When we arrived (on location)... a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company's protection system was functioning properly or not," he said.
The factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, according to search and rescue authorities.
On LinkedIn the company describes itself as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckz7: Watch: Suspected drug lord 'El Chapo Isidro' transferred to Mexico's capital
A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores and seven others were detained by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
Seven suspects were killed in the operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, the secretariat added.

Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.
Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.

Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained by Mexican special forces on Friday

Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores, the secretariat continued.
Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.
Eight people in total were arrested, including Meza Flores' second-in-command, who is also his cousin, and his brother-in-law, who is the group's financial operator, the secretariat added.
Watch: Moment Mexican reporter takes cover on air as gunshots ring out nearby
Meza Flores, his cousin, and his brother-in-law were flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said. The other five remained in the state of Sinaloa.
Authorities also said they had seized multiple weapons during the operation, including a grenade launcher, as well as drugs and cash.

The US Consulate General in the city of Hermosillo said it was "monitoring reports of ongoing security operations, armed clashes, road blockades, and vehicle fires that occurred overnight in Ahome, Guamúchil, Guasave, and Navolato" following the arrest of Meza-Flores.
It advised US citizens to remain alert for potential violence in the area and for residents to remain sheltered in place.
When Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.
Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.
He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.
The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.
A number of vehicles were pictured burning on a highway near Los Mochis, Sinaloa, after Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was arrested
Meza Flores was originally a high-ranking member of the Beltrán Leyva Organization, but a split between rival factions led to a surge of violence and prompted him to establish his own cartel by 2013.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8e3: Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.
His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.
Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.
The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".
The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.

Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.
Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.

The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.
The business broke into luxury markets and diversified beyond jewellery into watches, perfumes, leather goods and hotels.

"Paolo Bulgari began collaborating with his father in 1960, specialising in the knowledge of precious stones, of which he was one of the world's leading experts, and refining the sensibility and aesthetic sense that are at the root of the Bvlgari style," the Bvlgari company posted on social media. , external
"He poured his heart into his craft and into nurturing the talents of young designers, leaving an indelible mark on the world of jewellery.
"Thank you, Mr. Paolo, your legacy as a brilliant beacon of creative inspiration will continue to inspire generations to come."
Paolo Bulgari alongside David Bowie and his wife Iman in September 1991 in Versailles, France.
The post included a quote from Paolo Bulgari: "Everything can be a source of inspiration. There are no rules in creativity. Never."
The designer brand's celebrity clients have included Elizabeth Taylor, Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe, Ingrid Bergman, Sophie Loren, Anne Hathaway, Zendaya and Rihanna.
Actor Zendaya wearing a Bvlgari necklace at the 2025 Golden Globe awards.
In 2011 the family sold its controlling stake to the French luxury group LVMH, in a deal worth about 3.7 billion euros.
Chairman and CEO of LVMH, Bernard Arnault - who is one of the world's richest people - offered his condolences and also paid tribute to Paolo Bulgari.

"Throughout his life, he was a key architect of the brand's success, while simultaneously upholding and embodying the Italian spirit and the deeply Roman heritage of our exceptional jewellery Maison," he said in a statement to the BBC.
In 2019, Paolo Bulgari and his wife established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation to support young people through schooling and job training in disadvantaged neighbourhoods on the outskirts of Rome.

New Zealand was ready to support a draft deal that prompted UN climate talks to collapse without a decision.
COP31 ended on Monday in Antalya, Türkiye, with no consensus after more than two weeks of fraught negotiations.
The final draft deal, known as a cover decision, avoided any mention of the fossil fuels driving global warming.
The European Union, together with Panama and several other countries, formally objected to the draft, saying it was "unconscionable" to support it.
A spokesperson for New Zealand's caretaker climate minister, Simon Watts, said New Zealand was "ready to support a consensus on the cover decision".
Asked to confirm if that meant New Zealand supported the final draft as it stood, the spokesperson said: "Yes - New Zealand would have supported consensus in the room."

Despite the lack of a decision, the conference - which Watts attended for three days last week - was "a valuable opportunity for New Zealand to engage internationally and strengthen important relationships", the spokesperson said.
Green MP Francisco Hernandez, who was at COP31 until this morning NZT, said the EU and others were right to reject the draft decision.
The lack of any language about a transition away from fossil fuels was especially disappointing, he said.

"That was probably the most egregious thing for us - not naming fossil fuel as the thing that's causing climate change is basically like going to a cancer conference and not acknowledging smoking as the cause of lung cancer," he said.
The language about finance to assist vulnerable countries to adapt to climate change was also too weak, he said.
"There were some positive things in the text - things like the electrification target of 35 percent by 2035 - but unfortunately there was no real language there that it had to be clean energy."
The EU and others were right to walk away from the deal, he said.
"The draft text was just so weak - it doesn't meet the moment."
There were rumours all weekend that the deal would not pass, and a "febrile" atmosphere among the negotiating teams.
The failure to agree in a cover decision did not mean COP31 itself had failed, he said.
"I think people would be remiss to come away ... with the impression that we need to do less on climate, not more... This COP failed because it wasn't ambitious enough."
However, there was "probably merit" in considering whether the format of climate COPs - particularly the requirement for consensus decision-making - needed a second look.

"It really doesn't make sense to allow a small group of fossil fuel producers to hold the rest of the world hostage... Saudi Arabia was quite aggressive in trying to block progress on any of the texts."
Otago University climate and energy researcher Sebastian Gehricke said he had paid less attention to the annual talks in recent years because of how frustrating he found them.
"The word 'fossil fuels' in itself has been a hot topic, and that seems farcical to me because that's the whole point - the key driver of mitigating climate change is to reduce use of fossil fuels."
Even when the talks did result in deals or goals being set, there was a lack of follow-through.
"You look at the climate finance pledge, where developed nations promised to provide financing for climate projects for adaptation and mitigation of US$100 billion per year, and that was never hit.
"Then they upped the promise to $300 billion, which also seemed silly because they'd never met the [first] goal."

Thousands of kilometres from his PhD studies in Christchurch, Sunil Tamang's heart remains with his people in Nepal.
He has just returned from helping communities devastated by the deadly flash floods - more than a decade after doing the same following the earthquakes there.

He admits to The Detail that it was a harrowing and heartbreaking trek back to his home country, which began five days after the flash floods hit on 26 August, and finished just a couple of weeks ago.
"We lost so many people... almost 400 people that I personally knew, and so every day was a funeral ritual," he says.
"So for 49 days I was just attending one funeral after another, and sometimes in a day...10 to 15 funeral rituals.
"Sometimes it was for an individual, sometimes a group. Sometimes it's communal with... 52 people. So, I was on a wave of funeral rituals.

"It's a very roller coaster time because all of a sudden you feel happy to see all the surviving people... you kind of feel 'oh, they survived', but then as you talk to them you also realise that so many people that you know are not going to come back."

In Tibet, 43 people died, with more than 500 on the missing list. Some victims were swept 250 kilometres into neighbouring India.

"Our village is completely obliterated, completely destroyed, now completely a floodplain - just a barren rock. Nothing exists there. Just from my home village, we lost 181 locals - mostly close relatives and friends... no one survived... during this disaster.

"When I saw my hometown... I didn't even realise that my eyes were full of tears and... my body was super cold and it was shivering, and then my friend gave me a hug, and then I realised... how bad it is."
Sunil's hometown, Syaphru Besi, in 2011 (L) and after the 2026 floods (R).
Tsunami-like walls of water destroyed the Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border and struck dozens of settlements along a 72 km stretch of the Trishuli River on the morning of 26 August.
But nearly three months on, rebuilding has not been straightforward. Some of the houses Tamang rebuilt after the 2015 earthquakes can not be fixed this time round.
"We lost houses then, but we still had the land, so we could go back and somehow managed to rebuild. But now we don't have the land.
"And in some areas, it is completely unsafe. There is no possibility to rebuild there. That is the reality now, at least in my part of the village - I don't think that's possible."
"I think there is a need for the government to figure out some kind of solution with very, very close consultation with the local community.
"It's not just about losing your people, but you are also losing a place that holds so much to you... and being an indigenous community, this is really, really important."
He says about US$5 billion is required for the reconstruction recovery, but "we don't have that money - that's almost 10 percent of GDP for Nepal".
"We have got a lot of sympathies and support - emotional support - from international communities, but we also need to materialise this... with real help on the ground."

He was a highly influential figure in Australia's music industry as a critic, producer, interviewer and television presenter.
Australian Molly Meldrum, the former host of Countdown, has died aged 83.
For decades, if Meldrum urged viewers to "do yourself a favour" and buy your record, you knew you had made it in the music business.
Meldrum was a highly influential figure in Australia's music industry as a critic, producer, interviewer and television presenter.
As the host of Countdown, Molly Meldrum held extraordinary sway over what music Australian young people listened to.
The sold-out show at Melbourne’s Rod Laver Arena was held to raise funds for Head and Neck Cancer Australia, following Farnham’s own health battle in 2022.
‘You're The Voice’ is bigger than a pop song: the unofficial anthem still inspires singalongs at pubs, stadiums and festival fields decades later.
Rose Tattoo frontman Angry Anderson has died just weeks after being admitted to a hospital in Germany during the Australian rock band's European tour.

As the host of the ABC's music show Countdown, he brought the world's biggest pop stars into people's homes, and recorded some of the most iconic — if sometimes chaotic — interviews ever broadcast on Australian television.

Instantly recognisable in his trademark cowboy hat, Meldrum was described by some as "the most important person in pop", whose influence on the chart success of performers — particularly Australians — could not be overstated.
The ABC spoke to a close friend of Molly Meldrum's who said he had been in a Melbourne hospital for a number of days before dying.
Ian "Molly" Meldrum was born in Orbost, in regional Victoria, on January 29, 1943.
He spent the first 10 years of his life in the small country town before moving to the even smaller country town of Quambatook to live with his grandmother.
"My grandmother was one of my biggest influences on my life and I lived a fair bit with her and I absolutely adored my grandmother," he said.
"She taught me one of the great things that I've tried to live my life by and she told me that no-one's above you and no-one's below you and you should treat all people as equal."
Meldrum's interest in music surged when The Beatles toured Australia in 1964, taking the country by storm.
Meldrum and his friend Ronnie Burns — who would later have a successful recording career of his own — were kicked out of The Beatles' concert in Melbourne for being "too enthusiastic".

Just a few years later, Meldrum, who had been writing for Go-Set magazine and working on local TV shows, relocated to London to document Australian band The Groop's attempts to crack the UK music scene.
It was there that he got the scoop that took his career to a new level, securing an interview with John Lennon during which the Beatle dropped the bombshell that the band was splitting up.
"The story later went worldwide on radio, in Rolling Stone, everywhere," Meldrum said in 1981.
Meldrum had also been learning the ropes as a music producer, assisting with the recording of music by artists such as The Masters Apprentices.
Molly Meldrum worked as a reporter for Go-Set magazine in the 1960s and 1970s.
In 1969 he produced Russell Morris's recording of The Real Thing, transforming the song, which was written by Johnny Young as an acoustic ballad, into a six-minute, effects-laden epic.
The song was a number one hit domestically and is widely regarded as a milestone in music production in Australia.
Meldrum had experience as a television music reporter, but taking a job with brand new ABC music show Countdown was to be the single most important move in his career.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/environment_c: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/environment_climate/2734804%2Fcop-flop-scientist-warns-countries-are-losing-faith-in-un-climate-summits-as-deal-talks-stall
A climate scientist warns COP31 risks being seen as "a flop".
A New Zealand climate scientist says many countries are losing faith in the UN's annual climate summits, with the deal at COP31 teetering on collapse.
He said Pacific Island nations were among those who were deeply frustrated with this year's summit, as they face an "existential threat" of 1.5 degrees of global warming .
Fraught negotiations at COP31 in Türkiye have run more than a day over deadline, with international publications reporting a major deadlock overnight.
Talks stalled when a draft of the deal contained no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuels, The Guardian reported.
EU, Pacific Island and African states were pushing for the wording, while Saudi Arabia was among those understood to be pushing against it.
Then, at a late-night session, COP31 presidents Australia and Türkiye announced a new package aimed at achieving consensus.
President Murat Kurum said he believed concerns around fossil fuel wording had been solved, as had those around providing funding developing countries' climate change adaptation programmes.
"I truly remain hopeful, I still believe that we can arrive at some excellent decisions here in this hall, here in Antalya.
"The gap between us is narrowing, and the political will required to build a bridge exists right here in this room," he told the BBC.
A third draft of the deal has been sent to delegates in the early hours of the morning.

COP31 had been dubbed the "Implementation COP", with a focus on action for climate change financing and adaptation, Victoria University's Professor of Earth Sciences Tim Naish, who attended the summit as Chair of the World Climate Research Programme, said.
Instead, it had been one of the least productive ever and would be a failure if no deal was reached.
"It was a given that we would continue this so-called roadmap of transitioning away from fossil fuels that people thought wouldn't be controversial.
"What can happen at this COP is, essentially it's a flop, and we don't get any traction on the core goals that were set going into this process."

Naish said even if a deal was reached, he did not expect it to be transformative as the summit had "backslid" on major issues. Meanwhile, the world was getting closer to the Paris Agreement target of 1.5C degrees of warming , he added.
He said Pacific Island nations, who had a very strong voice at COP, were especially frustrated.
Cook Islands Prime Minister Mark Brown addresses leaders at PRECOP31 discussions in Fiji.
"This is why they are at the COP, 1.5 degrees is existential for them."

One of the world's biggest polluters, the United States, was not there, and climate change was getting less public attention amidst other major geopolitical issues and a general sense the 1.5 degrees target couldn't be reached.

"Bottom line is I think people are losing faith in the process, they are not seeing the process working, but I think the majority would be very loathe to leave it, because it's all we've got at the moment."

Karan Titus, a researcher in renewable energy engineering at the University of Canterbury who also attended COP31, said lack of pathways for climate adaptation finance had been a big weakness in the negotiations up till now.

Titus said he thought carbon capture and storage was being used as a way to solve the fossil fuel wording deadlock, but in his view this technology risked lock-in of fossil fuel projects for many years.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crm4: Keeping yourself warm by wearing thick clothes, using blankets and having hot drinks can help reduce heating bills
Energy prices are forecast to rise by 26% for millions of homes in January, but experts say there are ways to keep a check on rising bills.
Energy regulator Ofgem's price cap, as well as suppliers' fixed deals, set a limit on the price of each unit of energy, not the total bill.
So, you pay for what you use. Millions of people have cut back on their energy consumption during years of relatively high prices.
With the unit price of gas, in particular, set to soar, experts say you should take a fresh look at your energy use and renew good habits.
turning down the flow temperature on a combi boiler - usually indicated by a radiator icon, to make it operate more efficiently
turning off the pre-heat facility on some combi boilers, which would have kept some water heated up when not in use
turning down the thermostat one degree, although 18C is the recommended minimum
These are small changes but - alongside washing clothes at 30C, blocking draughts and batch cooking - they can reduce energy use and bills.
Ofgem says about five million people still pay their bill when it arrives every three months, rather than receive a monthly bill often initially based on an estimate.
Taking regular meter readings, or having a smart meter, while paying by monthly direct debit solves that problem.
Paying by direct debit costs significantly less than by so-called standard credit - typically £138 cheaper a year.

Customers on prepayment schemes - usually people on low incomes struggling to pay bills - used to pay a higher rate than others, but now they pay slightly less than the capped direct debit variable rate.
Various deals may rely on paying by direct debit or having a smart meter.

Moving to a fixed energy tariff means the price you are charged per unit of gas or electricity does not change every three months, although the total bill will still vary depending on how much energy you use.
The trouble is that it is very difficult to work out whether a fixed deal is a good deal at the moment, for those renewing fixed deals or looking for one for the first time.

Some fixed deals are available at unit prices below the next forecast price cap level. But should energy prices fall sharply then a longer-term fix might not seem such good value compared with the price cap.

So consumer group Which? also recommends paying close attention to any exit fees when picking a fixed deal. If variable prices fall below your fixed rate and you want to get out of it before the end of your agreement period, you may have to pay a hefty sum.
Before you fix, consumer website MoneySavingExpert advises you look at all the deals available , not just what your own supplier is offering.

The government will give a £100 payment to millions of homes to help cover winter energy costs. It will go to homes in council tax bands A to D in England, with the equivalent expected in Scotland and Wales.
There are also a range of other forms of support specifically for people on low incomes .
This winter anyone on means-tested benefits will get £150 off their electricity bill.
Your supplier will apply the discount automatically unless you are in Scotland, where you will need to contact your energy company to ask for the help.
Some people will also be eligible for a Cold Weather Payment , external and most pensioners will receive the winter fuel payment.
Beyond that, most energy suppliers offer hardship grants for people struggling to pay their bills and the government's Fuel Direct Scheme , external can help you repay energy debt.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4g: The future of Poundland hangs in the balance as it faces a possible collapse into administration.
Its owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, put it up for sale in September, but then rejected offers to keep the business afloat.
Poundland has a major presence on the High Street, with 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades under the Dealz brand.
If it were to collapse, the jobs of its 11,000 employees would be at risk, as well as potentially thousands of others at firms that supply the retailer.
People have not stopped shopping at Poundland - quite the opposite.

Although the chain was struggling when it was sold by Pepco last year for £1, the business turned a corner over the year to September, going from a £68m loss to an £18.1m profit before interest, tax and certain accounting charges.
Going into the vital Christmas period, first-quarter like-for-like sales were up 7% and operational profits of £1.9m were up £1.2m on last year.
Halloween sales were 11.4% higher than last year - this is usually a good indicator of how a retailer will do at Christmas, says retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth of Savvy Marketing.
According to Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency specialist Begbies Traynor: "This isn't a story about shoppers abandoning Poundland. The tills are busier than they were a year ago."
She adds: "On the face of it, a turnaround seems well under way."
However, Gordon Brothers has been restricting Poundland's access to cash needed to restock stores and meet day-to-day expenses.
It had frozen about £50m in funds leading to concerns Poundland's shops would run out of stock.
Gordon Brothers released around £21m over two weeks recently, giving the chain a little more breathing space.
Poundland seems to be facing "a funding and ownership problem rather than a trading collapse", Palmer says.

However, while Poundland boss Barry Williams says the business is making a "strong recovery", Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".
It says it has provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.
It has also made about £18m from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.
As well as being Poundland's owner, it is one of its lenders, and is owed loans, including a £22.5m shareholder loan it inherited when it bought the business for £1.
As the main creditor, Gordon Brothers would be first in line to get paid back if the business goes under - but its suppliers are not.

"When the owner is also the main lender, its first priority is recovering [loans]," says Palmer. "Sometimes the route that best protects the lender is different from the one that saves the most jobs, and that tension is why this has become such a political story."

Irish firm Martin Property Group has offered to buy the business as a going concern, while London-based holding company Xyra Group has also made a rescue bid , although doubts remain about the credibility of Xyra's offer.
A German investment firm, Zachert Private Equity, is also understood to have made a late offer.
Gordon Brothers has also been weighing options to break Poundland up.

The US company's view is that ultimately breaking the retailer up will provide more security for employees in the long term, because any buyers of its store estate will also have to agree to keep the employees on.
Insiders who are critical of how Gordon Brothers has handled the Poundland sale say it is driving the business into the ground to make money through the insolvency process.

What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash?

One AI worker, employed by one of the largest companies in the city, is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.
He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.
But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"
Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".

Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.
"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."
If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.
That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.

One study , external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.
But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.
For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.

"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvly: The disability minister has been looking into disability benefits for a year for his review, which is to be published on Tuesday

A review into the personal independence payment (Pip) will call for a "fundamental overhaul" of the assessment process to "better recognise people's varying costs and needs", the disability minister has said.
Sir Stephen Timms has been looking into disability benefits in England and Wales for the past year and found the set up was "no longer fit for purpose".
Writing in the Times , external , he said his review, to be published on Tuesday, would recommend people with the most severe conditions have a "fast track" process which is "less burdensome".
It comes after a separate review into young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) recommended Pip be scrapped and replaced for under-25s.

Sir Stephen, who produced his report alongside disability groups, carers, clinicians and MPs, said that while Pip had the "right aims" when it was created, there have been "marked shifts in the nature of disability and ill health" in the 13 years since.
He said there had been "substantial growth in claims for mental health and neurodiverse conditions as well as changes to wider society and the workplace".
"For those with the most severe conditions and end of life care, the review recommends a fast track which is less burdensome, with assessment capacity freed up for other cases.
"Where claimants do not have additional costs or care needs, we should be signposting them to services and support."
He added: "Someone with a lifelong or degenerative illness should not need regular reassessments which feel adversarial and unnecessary.

"Disabled people must have the chance to participate fully in everyday life, including in work, and need a more personalised, flexible system that supports them to do so, rather than itself being a barrier."
The Timms review was commissioned after a U-turn from former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government on a plan for major benefit reform in an attempt to reduce the welfare bill by £5bn a year.
More than 130 MPs, including 120 from Labour, signed an amendment to reject plans to cut disability and sickness-related benefit payments in 2025.
The rebels said they opposed the plans because of the number of people expected to be pushed into relative poverty and a lack of consultation at the time.

Sir Stephen's long-awaited review comes only a week after a former Labour Health Secretary Alan Milburn handed down his proposed reforms to tackle youth unemployment .
The government welcomed the Milburn review, which included a recommendation to move those aged 18 to 24 off Pip and the health element of universal credit, and onto an entirely new benefits system.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he thought the "same philosophy" could be applied "right through the age range".
At this stage it is unclear how both of the reviews will complement one another.

The cost of Pip is expected to rise to more than £41bn by 2030, up from £15bn in 2020. It was being claimed by 4m people in the UK as of 30 April 2026, according to the Department for Work and Pensions.
Though reforming the benefit has frequently been looked at as a way to reduce the Treasury's welfare bill, disability charities have described it as a lifeline for many.
Ahead of the Timms review being handed down, disability equality charity Scope said ministers must ensure Pip is not weakened.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6n9: Thousands of customers were affected by supply disruptions during high temperatures in May
South East Water has reported a half-year loss after penalties and £29m of costs following disruption to water supplies over the summer.

The company, which serves about 2.4 million customers across south-east England, recorded a pre-tax loss of £22.9m in the six months to 30 September, compared with a profit of £18.2m during the same period last year.
In July, regulator Ofwat ordered the company to spend £30.5m on improvements after supply interruptions hit customers across Kent and Sussex which affected more than 286,000 customers.
The company spent £29m responding to further supply interruptions during summer heatwaves in Kent and Sussex .
This included providing bottled water, setting up emergency water stations and compensating customers.
South East Water said it had set aside £14.6m in its latest financial results to cover the redress package.
The company supplies water to customers in Kent, East and West Sussex, Surrey, Hampshire and Berkshire.
Hosepipe bans remain in force across all areas supplied by South East Water.
In October, it was forced to ask shareholders for £50m after warning earlier in the year that it required additional funding in order to stay afloat.
The company said there were "early signs of improvement" following changes to its leadership team and plans for a "significant transformation" of the business.
Earlier this year, John Halsall was appointed chief executive after former chief executive David Hinton and chair Chris Train stepped down .
The departures followed criticism from MPs who said they had "no confidence" in the company's leadership after a review of repeated supply outages.
Richard Morse is due to become chair of the company on 3 December, succeeding interim chair Lisa Clement.
South East Water said the initial signs were "encouraging", although it warned improvements would take time to become fully visible to customers.
A spokesperson for the company said: "We know that customers will not judge us on the number of initiatives we launch or the promises we make.

"They will judge us on whether their water supply is more reliable, whether we communicate better and whether we provide the right support when they need it – we look forward to providing the evidence in future results."
