The San Francisco 49ers and Buffalo Bills remain the pacesetters in each conference of the NFL after both won again.
The 49ers beat the Minnesota Vikings in the last of a record nine international games this season to take their record to 9-1.
They lead the way in the NFC, with the Chicago Bears and their divisional rivals the Detroit Lions next best on 8-2.
Buffalo improved to 9-1 for the first time since 1991 and lead the AFC from another pair of divisional rivals, with the Kansas City Chiefs and Denver Broncos on 8-2.
The Chiefs and Broncos could be joined by the Cincinnati Bengals, who conclude week 11 at the Washington Commanders on Monday.
Mexico hosted the first regular-season game to be played outside the US in October 2005, and the NFL returned to the country on Sunday following a four-year absence.

After being redeveloped for the 2026 World Cup, the Azteca Stadium staged its sixth NFL game and the third involving San Francisco, who kicked off this season's international series by beating the Los Angeles Rams in Australia in week one.
Sunday's game pitted the league's best offence against the best defence and was the first international game to be played in the primetime slot.
The Vikings defence had not conceded more than 23 points in a game this season, but the 49ers offence outsmarted them in front of 85,612 fans in Mexico City.
The 49ers scored four touchdowns in the first half - two by George Kittle - before running out 35-10 winners.
Mike Evans returned after missing three games with an Achilles problem to finish with 109 receiving yards and a touchdown.
With the game played at high altitude - about 7,220ft (2,240m) above sea level - some players used oxygen masks on the sidelines.
San Francisco face another test of their Super Bowl credentials next Sunday at home to the defending champions, the 6-4 Seattle Seahawks, who were one of six teams on their bye this week.
The Jacksonville Jaguars entered week 11 with the best regular-season record over the past 12 months - they had lost only twice - and had scored more than 30 points in each of their past four games.
Yet the New York Giants managed to stifle the Jaguars for three quarters and led 20-6 heading into what proved to be a dramatic final quarter.
The Jaguars had to settle for a field goal after a controversial call denied them a touchdown, but they still threatened a fightback as they cut the deficit to five.
The Giants offence did enough to stop the Jags getting one more possession, though, and secure a 23-18 home win.
It was the first time the NFC East leaders have beaten a team with a winning record this season and they are now 6-3-1, while the 7-3 Jags remain in charge of the AFC South.
In his first season as head coach, John Harbaugh could lead the Giants to their first division title since 2011, when 'Big Blue' went on to claim their fourth Super Bowl.
They remain clear of the 5-6 Dallas Cowboys, whose rollercoaster season continued with a 51-30 win over the Tennessee Titans, with Dak Prescott throwing for 325 yards and four touchdowns.
Cam Skattebo earned a first down to secure victory for the Giants before celebrating with a backflip
Although Josh Allen threw for more interceptions than touchdowns (2-1), the Bills were still comfortable, beating the Miami Dolphins 26-9 for their sixth straight victory.
The Bills have a mouth-watering Thanksgiving clash on Thursday (01:20 GMT, Friday) at home to the Kansas City Chiefs, who beat the Arizona Cardinals 34-7.
Travis Kelce had two scores for the Chiefs, claiming multiple touchdowns in the same game for the first time since a play-off win over Buffalo in January 2024.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Kansas City Current, who were formed in 2020, won this year's National Women's Soccer League championship
Sarah Jones Simmer, chief operating officer of the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL), could not wait for the championship game between Washington Spirit and Kansas City Current on Saturday night.
The NWSL showpiece was played out in front of a sellout crowd of more than 19,000 at Audi Field in Washington DC, with tickets retailing at more than $300 (£229).
Ultimately, the Current triumphed 2-1 to clinch their first title, condemning Spirit to an unwanted record of three lost finals in a row.

Just a few hours earlier on this side of the Atlantic, Alexia Putellas, who last month was crowned the best player in the world for the third time at the Ballon d'Or ceremony, was scoring twice for London City against Crystal Palace in front of 4,000 people in Bromley.
It is a totally unfair comparison. After all, a championship final is the type of jamboree the USA does particularly well.
Nevertheless, women's football is booming in America at the moment, with attendance figures at record highs, more franchises joining the league and club retail sales double those of 2025.
The US is the most successful nation in women's international football.

The four-time World Cup winners (1991, 1999, 2015 and 2019) and five-time Olympic gold medallists, the nation of Mia Hamm, Alex Morgan and Megan Rapinoe, has a history of winning - and the domestic game is key.
"If anything, soccer is more seen as a women's sport [in the USA]," says broadcaster Jacqui Oatley, who currently commentates on the NWSL for ESPN.
"Women have won World Cups and Olympic Games - and the men have been nowhere near as successful."
While teams in the United States became professional in 2001 - for WSL teams it was 2018 - the top flight has taken several different guises over the years.
The current NWSL kicked off in 2013 as an eight-team competition, and has since expanded to 16 franchises, with two more joining from 2028.
There is no relegation and Kansas City's victory on Saturday means the league has had eight different winners since its iteration.
As the below graph shows, the ownership picture for these sides is far more varied than in the UK, with American sides much less dependent on their male counterparts.

Indeed, Kansas City are blazing a trail. Established in December 2020, unaffiliated to a men's side and backed by ambitious owners that include Brittany Mahomes - the wife of NFL quarterback Patrick Mahomes.

Winning the championship is the crowning achievement for an ambitious franchise and such success is something independent London City hope to emulate in the UK. They are four points from the WSL summit nearly halfway through the 2026-27 season.

Kansas City were also the first club to build a bespoke stadium solely for women's football and the demand for seats at their 11,500-seater CPKC Stadium is huge. Earlier this year, Brighton announced their own purpose-built venue, planned for 2030-31.
"I think our independence is a hallmark of the league," says the NWSL's Jones Simmer.
"It is something we are very proud of. It allows us to invest in our own growth, prioritise the women's game and ensure resources are flowing to it."
It is markedly different from the UK set-up, where all WSL teams bar London City are, at least, affiliated and more often financially reliant on the men's side.
But that presents just as much of an opportunity, according to Jones Simmer.
"I know Nikki [Doucet, chief executive of the WSL] and I admire what she is building," she says.

"There's a really unique opportunity to build on the legacy of these 100-year-old men's clubs that are household names, to build women's brands that embrace the legacy but also have their own identity."
JJ Gabriel featured for Manchester United's senior team in pre-season
It has been one of the biggest transfer sagas of the year - around a player who has never played competitive football.
Forward JJ Gabriel, who has recently turned 16, walked out on Manchester United in September and now has a verbal agreement to join Real Madrid.
Before even playing a senior game - barring friendlies - he has told Spanish newspaper Marca his "dream is to win the Ballon d'Or".
Gabriel's real name is Joseph Junior Andreou O'Cearuill - with Cypriot and Irish lineage - but he changed his name, reportedly for commercial purposes.

His father, London-born Joe O'Cearuill, played twice for the Republic of Ireland - but the highest level he played at club level was a loan spell with Brighton in League One and one minute in the Uefa Cup with St Patrick's Athletic. He has been actively involved in his son's career.
Gabriel was scheduled to become Manchester United 's youngest ever player in the Carabao Cup against Brighton on 16 September, but had told the club he planned to leave by then.
How long will Gabriel have to wait for a first-team debut now? In the past 10 years Real have only handed two debuts to 17-year-olds and none to a 16-year-old.
When Real boss Jose Mourinho was asked about Gabriel on Friday, he said: "I don't have a feeling [about Gabriel]. I don't have a feeling with players who don't work with me."
In fact, Real have not even announced anything yet - despite Gabriel posting a 50-second video montage on social media saying goodbye to United this week.
Why schoolboys have become a huge part of football's transfer market
For a while now Madrid have been getting the best young talents early and turning them into Galacticos before they cost in excess of 100m euros.
Vinicius Junior and Rodrygo came that way, then Endrick - and Gabriel is seen as the next.
It fits the policy run by Jose Angel Sanchez, the director general, and Juni Calafat, head of scouting. It is a long-term bet on one of the most promising young players in the international game.
Barcelona looked at him too, and backed away because the commissions were too high. Madrid believe in the player so much that they were willing to pay whatever it took to get the deal done.
The expectations are very high and the aim is for him to reach the first team. They want him at Castilla - Real's reserve team - but the situation right now does not allow it.
Castilla and Real Madrid C cannot sign players until January, so for the time being he is expected to play for the Juvenil - the under-18s.

Madrid also learned from the Martin Odegaard period that training with the first team while playing for the B side is a bad idea. So the plan is a spell in the B side, and when he is ready, Gabriel jumps straight into the first team.

Where Madrid are less happy is with how things have unfolded. Madrid wanted to set the timing themselves and be discreet, because they do not want problems with Manchester United and do not want to upset anyone. At Real Madrid, nobody is bigger than the club.
The idea was to keep everything quiet until January and announce it then. But with Gabriel already training in Madrid, the secret was never going to last.
"Players are moving to him because his reputation is that he'll get you a move to a bigger club," one Premier League club source told BBC Sport.
Dubai-based Barat does not just consider himself a super-agent, but a "boutique" super-agent.
Born in Iran and raised in London, Barat says he fell into football almost by accident after many years in international business.
After initially working as an intermediary at low-level clubs, he founded Epic Sports in January 2020.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cricket/arti: India captain Shubman Gill says that players should be allowed to use saliva to shine the ball again, six years after it was outlawed.
The ban was first introduced by the International Cricket Council (ICC) as a result of the Covid-19 pandemic, in May 2020, before being made permanent in 2022.
Since then, players have been allowed to use sweat to shine the ball because there was less risk of transmitting the Covid disease.
Bowlers use saliva or sweat to polish one side of the ball while leaving the other side to deteriorate naturally, a process which helps bowlers swing the ball through the air.
Gill, 27, questioned why the ICC is yet to reverse the ban during his news conference after India's high-scoring draw against New Zealand in the first Test at Wellington.
"I don't know why ball shining [using saliva] is not allowed," said Gill, who scored 98 in India's only innings.
"It's been years since the Covid-19 pandemic passed, I don't know why it's not allowed now."

The older or more worn a cricket ball gets, the less it will swing and therefore becomes easier for batters to face, which is why bowlers aim to preserve the shine on one side for as long as possible.
New Zealand had slipped to 70-5 in their first innings before centuries from Henry Nicholls and Glenn Phillips led an incredible recovery to 386 all out.
India then piled on a mammoth 720-9 but were unable to force a victory on the final day as the Black Caps blocked out for a draw, with Gill saying the pitch lacked assistance for his bowlers.
"It's frustrating because we didn't get the result we wanted. Draws are not common, we are not used to draws," Gill added.
"Days three, four and five just got flatter and flatter. There was no impact of the overs being bowled on the wicket, or even the days being played. It just got slower."
The draw hurt both sides in their quest to finish in one of the top two spots in the World Test Championship table to secure a place in next June's final at the Oval in London.
South Africa and Australia are first and second with New Zealand third and India fourth.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Diego Simeone beat the record of Luis Aragones, who recorded his final La Liga victory in 2004
Atletico Madrid's 3-0 victory over Getafe may have been routine, but the win was another landmark in manager Diego Simeone's lengthy tenure at the club.
Sunday's triumph at Estadio Coliseum was the Argentine's 345th La Liga win in his 567th match, surpassing the record for the most victories in the Spanish top flight.
Simeone beat the mark of legendary former Atletico and Spain manager Luis Aragones, who won 344 matches but needed 189 more games to reach that total.
"It makes me happy," Simeone said of setting the new mark, with his side now third in the table after 10 wins from 13 games.
"I don't usually find many things to be happy about, but there is an incredible amount of work behind this."
Questioned about the perception that his team are defensive, Simeone said that was a "constant criticism we face".
He added: "I don't place much value on it, but I do take note of it.
"This narrative that we're a defensive team, as if we're always playing solely to defend. You don't win 345 matches just by defending. Is that even possible?"
The 56-year-old has been in charge of Atletico since December 2011, joining the club in an era when Jose Mourinho's Real Madrid and Pep Guardiola's Barcelona were the dominant teams in Spain.

He outlasted the pair of managerial superstars, leading Atletico into a period of consistent success and staying with his side long enough to witness Mourinho's return to Real this summer, 13 years after his initial departure.
Having won the Europa League in May 2012, after his appointment on 23 December 2011, Simeone led Atletico to the European Super Cup title three months later.
He then won the Copa del Rey in his first full season and secured the club's first La Liga title since 1996 - when Simeone was an Atletico player - in the following campaign.
Atletico have established themselves as the third force in Spanish football under his leadership, qualifying for the Champions League in every full season under his charge.

However he has been unable to win European football's premier competition, losing in the final to city rivals Real twice in heart-breaking fashion - in extra-time in 2014 after Real scored a stoppage-time equaliser, and on penalties in 2016.
Simeone's last silverware arrived in 2021 when he won a second Spanish league championship, while he also guided the team to a Europa League and Super Cup double in 2018.
His contract expires at the end of this season with the Atletico fanbase now waiting to see if their manager intends to extend his remarkable victory record into another campaign.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/: After Ireland's win over world champions South Africa on Saturday, Andy Farrell had one eye on the past, and another on what is to come.
It was a result that had left Ireland's head coach brimming with pride, as they ended a run of six straight defeats against either the Springboks, New Zealand or France.

With the World Cup now just 10 months away, it is all part of the bigger picture as Ireland aim to progress past the quarter-finals for the first time, with the ultimate goal of lifting the Webb Ellis Cup.
"Whether we lose by three or win by three, you understand how you apply yourself in a big game like that, and it doesn't get any bigger," Farrell said after the 20-17 win.
"You're always trying to kick on to the next level, and sometimes you don't know what that level is because you've never been there as a group.
"But this group is like that. We're trying to do new things together, and it sets us up nicely to keep kicking on."

Farrell looked back to the opening three matches of the Nations Championship in July, when he handed a number of players minutes at international level against Australia and Japan - such as Nick Timoney, Tom Stewart and Tom Clarkson.
Those players played a key role in downing the Springboks in Dublin as second-half replacements.
"We chose to take players to the Southern Hemisphere who had not had that type of experience.
"It's never going to be smelling of roses in that regard [performances over 80 minutes], so you end up where you're at, but we grew as a group, so therefore it's priceless for us."
Ireland beat the Boks: Post-match reaction with Josh Van der Flier and Mike McCarthy
Given how the tables were weighted, Ireland would have topped the southern hemisphere table by two points.
But the northern hemisphere's domination of the inaugural competition meant a more condensed table, and a fifth-place play-off against Australia will be their reward.
But Friday will be another tough test against a Wallabies side who were one missed penalty away from beating Ireland in Sydney in July.
Speaking before he knew who Ireland would be playing, and when, Farrell denied that playing for fifth place would be an anti-climax.
"We've got another week of international rugby together. We're in the green shirt, and that's special and it's a privilege, so we'll look forward to that."
Ireland's team selection to face South Africa had a surprise as captain Dan Sheehan, who usually plays at hooker, was named to start at number eight.
It was only his second professional start in the back row, with his first outing coming for Leinster against Munster before the international window.
Farrell's decision was certainly justified as Sheehan more than played his role in a scrum that held its own against the world-leading Springbok pack.
"He's so calm, isn't he? I spoke to him over the last couple of weeks about all sorts of things, about number eight, but he wasn't worried and it doesn't bother him in the slightest," said Farrell.
"It's like, 'why are you asking me that question?'. It's almost like an insult. He's so calm, he's such a gifted rugby player.
"That's his character. He just sees it for what it is and he gets on with it. That calm and influence has a knock-on effect that goes through the team."
Another standout for Ireland was Jamison Gibson-Park, whose experience and guile helped the hosts get over the line as the Boks piled on late pressure.
One clearing kick, from his own try line to the halfway line, was a particular standout in a game filled with classy moments.
Farrell described the 34-year-old's kicking as "immense", and said he is getting better with each passing year.
Prop Rhys Carre came off the bench for Wales against Japan in Cardiff
Wales head coach Steve Tandy, with one eye on the World Cup, vowed to rotate his side for Nations Championship finals weekend even before his side had faced Australia.
Hopes of an autumn clean sweep - something only achieved once in 2018 under Warren Gatland - were dashed by the Wallabies at the Principality Stadium on Saturday.
Wales dust themselves down before finishing the November campaign against familiar foes Japan on Saturday (13:10 GMT).
The Six Nations is not a time for experimenting, so it presents a rare chance to have a look at players in the countdown to next year's World Cup in Australia.
Wales spluttered to victory against Eddie Jones' side at the start of the month and will expect a more comfortable success at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium.
The fixture, a fifth meeting with the Brave Blossoms in 16 months, presents a chance for Tandy to test his squad depth.

Eleven of Wales' players started against Japan, New Zealand and Australia - Blair Murray, Louis Rees-Zammit, Eddie James, Max Llewellyn, Sam Costelow, Tomos Williams, Nicky Smith, Dewi Lake, Archie Griffin, Dafydd Jenkins and Jac Morgan.
It is fair to assume that plenty of big hitters will watch from the stands at Twickenham, after the mental and physical demands of the past fortnight.
"I can rotate the team and we'll still put in a performance. It doesn't matter who wears the shirt, we've got to perform," said Tandy.
"Whenever we put a team out, the objective is to win a Test match. That will be no different next Saturday."
The core of the first-choice team will remain in England after the Japan game and rejoin their clubs in the Prem.
Former Wales and Lions wing Alex Cuthbert urged Tandy to resist the temptation to give the frontline players a breather.
"We need to put our best team out. We really want to put a marker down against Japan," he said on the Scrum V podcast.
"It's an opportunity to really put Japan to the sword if we really want to take some momentum into the Six Nations."
The Japanese are stretched by injury and conceded 24 tries in defeats by England and Scotland.
Wales fielded the same starting line-up against Japan and Australia either side of the New Zealand victory.
Man of the match against the All Blacks James Botham went from the XV to missing out completely against the Wallabies, much to the frustration of his father Liam.
Botham's fellow Cardiff back-row forward Taine Basham and Leicester wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb suffered the same fate.
Versatile forward Taine Plumtree has proved his worth from the bench in the past two fixtures but might hope for a first Test start since Scotland in the third round of the 2026 Six Nations.
Tandy is spoilt for choice in the back-row and gave promising Exeter flanker Kane James a second cap off the bench against the Wallabies.

Wales have also developed depth at loose-head prop to the extent that strong-running Rhys Carre, Welsh Rugby Writers' Association (WRWA) player of the year after his Six Nations exploits, missed out against New Zealand and Australia.
Smith has started all three November Tests and Ospreys' Gareth Thomas has been strong off the bench.

Wales selected three uncapped players in their initial Nations Championship squad with Cardiff loose-head prop Rhys Barratt, who played against the Barbarians in the summer, joined by the Dragons pair of scrum-half Che Hope and centre Aneurin Owen.
That figure became four when in-form Scarlets wing Macs Page got a call-up due to Rio Dyer's hamstring injury.
Tandy has given first caps to nine players since taking the reins in the summer of 2025 and could hit double figures at Twickenham.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/2738317: The best of the batting conditions are likely to be over as the Black Caps attempt to save the first test against India.
New Zealand will resume their second innings on 119 for two, still trailing India by 233 runs and facing 90 overs on what could be a variable wicket on the final day at the Basin Reserve.
"We're pretty behind the game, obviously," Rachin Ravindra said at the end of the day. "It was a good period to get through two down."

Ravindra and Devon Conway got through 23 overs to close out the fourth day having spent much of the previous two days watching India put on a record score of 720 for nine . There are unlikely to be as many fireworks from the New Zealand batters on Monday.
"For us it's about batting as long as we can, we know it's been a relatively good wicket, so hopefully we can apply ourselves for a long period of time and bat three sessions," Ravindra said.

"I'd probably be one of Dev's biggest supporters, he's such a good player but also class. Whenever he bats a number of balls, he continues on, so hopefully he can do that tomorrow.
"He's looking amazing, getting into great positions and assessing the bowlers really well. I don't want to touch the money, I'll touch wood, but he's looking very good."

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/2749948: Netball New Zealand says it's deeply saddened by the death of former Silver Ferns captain Julie Carter, aged 60.
A crafty goal attack, who could also slot in at wing attack, Carter played 50 Tests for New Zealand between 1986 and 1993.
She became the Silver Ferns' 16th captain when she took up the role in late 1992.
Carter first rose to prominence through the schoolgirl ranks in Waikato, where she was earmarked early as a future Silver Fern.
In 1986 she made her debut for the national side. After missing selection in 1987, she bounced straight back and became a regular in the black dress from 1988 to 1993.
As captain she led the Silver Ferns to 10 wins from 11 Tests, a record that reflected both her leadership and her competitive drive.
Carter is the second former Silver Fern captain to have died this year. In August, former Silver Fern captain Ana Noovao died aged 58, after a long illness .
Noovao, a midcourter, played for New Zealand between 1989 and 1992 and was named the 15th captain of the Silver Ferns, who she led for six Tests in 1992.
Carter's career spanned a period of change for the Silver Ferns, and she played a key part in building the foundations of a new era for the team.

Her career highlights included representing New Zealand in the demonstration match at the 1990 Commonwealth Games in Auckland, being a member of the Silver Ferns team that won silver at the 1991 World Championships in Sydney and winning a gold medal at the 1989 World Games in Germany.
Silver Fern #80 was known as one of the great thinkers of the game and was tough and uncompromising under the goal, while setting high standards for herself and those around her.

Carter played her domestic netball for Waikato before moving to Wellington in 1990. She later made the move further south and in 1998 and 1999 played for the Southern Sting in the Coca Cola Cup. Her side won the title in 1999 against the defending champion Otago Rebels.
After retiring, she remained involved in netball as a coach and inspiring the next generation of players.
Netball New Zealand extends its deepest sympathies to Julie's whānau, friends, former teammates and all who knew her.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/2749595: Analysis: The All Blacks coaches will show their players some confronting statistics from their defeat to England but are unlikely to dwell on the negatives at the end of what has clearly been a long and arduous year.

If the 37-12 scoreline at Twickenham - a record margin of defeat to a Northern Hemisphere nation - appeared bad enough, here are some other top-line numbers for the players and the team's supporters to get their heads around:
It is clear the All Blacks have fallen off a metaphorical cliff since their 43-21 victory over Scotland on 8 November. The question is why.

There were failures of leadership in their 35-28 loss to Wales but the drop-off in performance a week later when they had everything to play for against a side who beat them this time last year - including the celebrating of milestones for a couple of their veterans , not to mention playing for a place in the top Nations Championship final - has shocked Dave Rennie and his assistants.

Rennie has been reluctant to blame his players' lethargy on the trials of their tour of South Africa (and Baltimore) which included four tests played at the highest intensity along with four mid-week matches, but New Zealand Rugby chief executive Steve Lancaster was less reticent on Monday and on the same morning selector Sir Graham Henry stated: "we've just run out of petrol, quite frankly".
The sudden loss of All Blacks' security boss Logan Cadwallader at the start of the Scotland week should also be taken into account.
The All Blacks form a huddle after their record defeat at Twickenham.

Blaming the All Blacks' inability to maintain their Nations Championship form on the mental and physical peaks they had to ascend against the world champions in August and September may be overly convenient for their harshest critics but not agreeing with a theory does not automatically make it less valid.

So poor were the All Blacks in virtually every facet - apart from possibly their scrum and maul defence - and so easily were they physically dominated, that a few players having an off day or some players not being good enough in the first place does not stack up.
South Africa's corresponding drop-off lends weight to the idea that something else is in play.

The Springboks have also lost their last two tests - albeit more closely and against higher-ranked opponents in France and then Ireland. But they have also appeared lethargic, especially late in games, and, similarly to the All Blacks, have struggled to get their attack going.
There was also the not insignificant matter of the 'Boks losing to Australia recently in a bizarre test in Perth during which the Wallabies finished with only 11 players on the field.
"They've lost three of their last four," Rennie replied when asked about the 'Boks recent difficulties and the potential significance of 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' tour as a factor.

"Oh look, it was an unbelievable tour, the 'RGR'. Certainly, talking to a couple of the African boys post the fourth test they were saying it was the toughest month of their lives. Those tests were brutal. Perhaps it has taken a little bit of a toll but we're not trying to use that as an excuse. The tour was great for us - we learned a lot.
"I thought we performed well against Australia [for big wins in Auckland and Sydney]. Against Scotland we were reasonably solid and over the last two weeks we were well below par."

India have won the Slumberzone Indian Centenary Hockey Series after edging the Black Sticks Men 3-2 in the opening match on Friday and holding the home side to a pair of hard-fought 2-2 draws at Lloyd Elsmore Park in Auckland over the weekend.
The three-match series marked 100 years of sporting ties between India and New Zealand, dating back to 1926 when an Indian Army hockey team first toured the country.
That team was the first Indian hockey side to tour overseas and the first Indian sporting team to visit New Zealand.
It included Dhyan Chand, who went on to become one of the sport's most celebrated players.
The centenary celebrations also featured matches involving India's armed forces teams, who played five games in Wellington and Auckland as part of their tour.

The Indian Armed Forces team beat a Wellington selection 7-3 at Kāpiti Sports Turf on 14 November before overcoming a Governor-General's XI 5-3 at Wellington's National Hockey Stadium the following day.
On Thursday, the visitors continued their winning run with a commanding 4-1 victory over the New Zealand Defence Force.
They maintained that momentum over the weekend, winning both matches against the New Zealand Defence Force 3-1 on Saturday and 2-0 on Sunday.
The New Zealand Indian Sports Association women's team also completed a weekend double against the New Zealand Defence Force women's team, recording 3-1 and 4-1 victories in its two matches.
Saturday's programme also featured an exhibition kabaddi match, with a Māori women's team showcasing their skills alongside a team representing the Indian community in New Zealand.
India have claimed a hockey series against the Black Sticks with a win and two draws as the teams marked 100 years of sporting ties between the two nations.
On the international hockey front, the Black Sticks made strong starts in all three matches, opening the scoring each time, but India showed their resilience to fight back.
Saturday's encounter produced some exciting attacking hockey, with Dylan Thomas giving the hosts the lead through a moment of individual brilliance.
He weaved past defenders before squeezing the ball past the goalkeeper from a tight angle near goal.
India responded with an equaliser from Angad Singh before half-time to make it 1-1.
Sam Hiha restored the Black Sticks' advantage, but Indian captain Sanjay kept his side in the contest, converting a penalty corner late in the match to secure a 2-2 draw.
Sunday's series finale delivered another closely contested battle, with Thomas once again putting the Black Sticks ahead in the first quarter.
India gradually took control of possession and began creating attacking opportunities, with captain Sanjay finding the equaliser.
The visitors then struck again just two minutes later, with Selvam Karthi putting India ahead.
But the Black Sticks refused to go down without a fight, and Benji Culhane produced a superb individual effort in the final quarter to bring the hosts level at 2-2.
He dribbled into the circle along the right baseline before unleashing a powerful sweep across the face of goal, wrong-footing the Indian goalkeeper and squeezing the ball through a narrow gap.

"It's always nice to play hockey at home and really good to see the Auckland community and the wider hockey community come here and support all three games," said Black Sticks acting head coach Shea McAleese.
"Close games, all three of them, but unfortunately we just didn't quite get the W in the end today," he said.

The All Blacks were crushed 37-12 by England on Sunday morning at Twickenham, their heaviest ever defeat to the English, following last weekend's shock loss to Wales, their first in 73 years.
Dave Rennie's men looked tired and slow against England and they've now lost five games this year, just the third time in history the All Blacks have dropped that many games in a season.
They've also slipped to fifth in the world rankings, their equal lowest position of all-time.
Henry believes the All Blacks tour of South Africa, which included four tests against the Springboks, earlier this year has left them short of a gallop for their final few matches of the season.
"It's been the massive itinerary this year with the South African tour and the four provincial games and the four tests there. We've just run out of petrol."
Henry said the Springboks, who have also lost two tests on the trot, are also showing signs of fatigue.
"Look at South Africa, they've lost three of their last four games, so they're starting to run out of petrol as well. It's just accumulation of game after game after game."
All Blacks defence coach Tana Umaga (L) and selector Sir Graham Henry.
The All Blacks have played 16 games this year and this weekend's Nations Championship third place playoff against England at Twickenham will be their 17th.
Rennie now has a 7-5 win/loss record in 2025 for a 58.33 percent win rate, the fifth-worst record among the 28 test coaches New Zealand has had.
Despite falling to back to back defeats, Henry is confident Rennie is the right man to guide the All Blacks to next year's World Cup.
He said a long and intense season had taken its toll on the side.

"I've been really impressed with the quality of the people. The boys are fantastic and the staff are doing their best, but it's just too much. They've been asked to do too much, and they're trying their best."
Former All Blacks winger and now Sky Sport commentator, Jeff Wilson, agreed that the players looked tired during the England game, but questioned whether fatigue was a valid excuse.
"I've done the numbers on the number of games that a lot of these players had played up until this game and no one was pushing close to 30," Wilson said.

"Most of the guys had played less than 25 [over the entire year] and if you compare that to Northern Hemisphere teams or the South African sides, they're playing a huge number of games across the season."
Wilson wonders whether it's physical or emotional fatigue affecting the team, following the death of their long-time head of security Logan Cadwallader during their first week on tour.
"The question has to be asked where's that fatigue come from? And was it as much emotional fatigue as it was physical?"

Sir Graham Henry also believes other teams have caught up. He said England, Ireland, France and South Africa all had a chance to win next year's World Cup and questioned whether Super Rugby was a strong enough competition to prepare New Zealand players for test rugby.
"Other sides have got better. Their competitions below international rugby are much stronger than ours, they're producing a lot of players and they're playing a great brand of rugby."

New Zealand Rugby (NZR) has given its "full support" to All Blacks coach Dave Rennie, saying he's the right man for the job.

The All Blacks fell to a record 37-12 defeat to England on Sunday following last weekend's shock loss to Wales , raising questions about Rennie's ability to guide the team less than a year out from the World Cup.
NZR chief executive Steve Lancaster told RNZ's Morning Report that while the back-to-back losses are deeply disappointing, Rennie has NZR's unequivocal support.
"I've told Dave that and I'm happy to, you know, state that publicly that, you know, we, Dave has our full support," Lancaster said.
"We're confident that we have the right person coaching this team, no question in our minds."
Lancaster told Morning Report the All Blacks players also back Rennie and said there's no dissatisfaction with the coach within the team.

"I've had the benefit of being in this team environment over the course of this year and they're a very strong and aligned group. There's clear leadership. The team are behind Dave, but they know what they have to achieve."
"The last two weeks' performance is really disappointing and we need to understand how that's come to pass, but no question over Dave being the right person to lead the team."
Lancaster believes the All Blacks are showing signs of growth under Rennie. He said there have been some significant improvements over the season.

"In terms of what we're seeing within the team environment, within the way the team is performing, notwithstanding the last two weeks, which we're absolutely going to have to own and understand, we've seen some positive shifts."
The All Blacks looked flat against England and some pundits have questioned whether the players were fatigued after a long season, which involved a bruising four-test series against the Springboks .
Lancaster said he didn't want to make excuses, but said it's worth exploring whether fatigue played a role in the All Blacks' last two defeats.
"We probably, neither ourselves nor South Africa, fully appreciated just how gruelling that Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series was," Lancaster said.
"Those four tests were unbelievable in their intensity, the quality of the rugby, but South Africa have lost their last two matches, three of their last four and we've lost our last two.
"We will have to look deeper to understand whether that has been a factor or not and if it has, what we need to change to ensure that we don't see that again."

Lancaster said the death of the All Blacks head of security in Edinburgh in the first week of their Northern Tour had also affected the side, who he believes will be determined to beat England in this weekend's Nations Championship third-place playoff at Twickenham.

"There's no lack of resolve or motivation. There wasn't going into last week either, right? So that's kind of what makes it a little bit inexplicable, but the team will absolutely be doing everything they can to get up and finish the year on a positive note."

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/2740999: There were tears on board as the Black Foils put a difficult SailGP season behind them with victory in the penultimate round in Dubai.
It was the New Zealand team's third win at the event and first this season following a year when they spent four months off the water.
Peter Burling and his crew missed four events following a horror crash with Team France in Auckland in February.

"It's a real mixture of emotions," said Black Foils strategist Liv Mackay.

Mackay said the win reflected just how far the team had come since the start of the year.

The team was involved in a collision in the first race of the season in Perth, with Burling handed demerit points . The team then collided with Team France in the second round in Auckland, leaving two sailors needing hospital treatment .
Auckland was horrific, Mackay said. "From there we've rebuilt in a lot of different ways. In the four months we were out as a team, the fleet really progressed super quickly."
Black Foils co-chief executive and driver Burling was proud of how they've recovered this season.

"It means a whole heap for this team to come out after a bit of time off the water and put together the performance we did today. That really shows the level we can compete at and builds a lot of confidence amongst the group for next season," Burling said.
The Black Foils will compete in the final round in Abu Dhabi next weekend but won't be contenders for the overall title with Australia, Spain, Sweden and the US contesting the final.

Fiji claimed their first win in the Nations Championship following their 21-16 win over Italy in Udine on Sunday morning.
The result meant all three Pacific Island teams Fiji, Samoa and Tonga recorded wins at the weekend in their respective World Rugby internationals.
Tonga had thrashed Hong Kong China 55-19 in Hong Kong on Saturday night in their Nations Cup clash, while Samoa walloped Spain 90-22 earlier today.
In Udine, the story truly belonged to Fiji and their second half resurgence as the islanders romp to the victory, silencing the Italian crowd that had cheered their side on.
The result means the two teams will go head to head again in London in the weekend, with the two both finishing sixth in their respective South and Northern hemisphere pools.
Fiji scored three tries to Italy's one, with captain Tevita Ikanivere claiming two, while flanker and 'Player of the Match' Kitione Salawa adding another.
Flyhalves Ben Volavola and his replacement Caleb Muntz added the extra six points between them.
Italy scored their only try through captain Lorenzo Cannone, with fullback Tommaso Allan adding 11 points through a conversion and three penalties.
Man of the match performer Salawa said post-match the Italians were tough and thanked his fellow players for staying in the fight until the end.
"First of all I would like to than the Lord Almighty for giving us the strength today," he said.
"I would also like to thank the boys for the great effort against the Italian boys.
"Thank the Italian boys for giving us a hard battle tonight and our boys for staying in the fight."
Italy were fierce on defence and lightning on attack, keeping smiles on their fans' faces in the first half.
Fiji's Nathan Hughes was the first to receive the ball as Italy kicked off and the two teams tested each other out in the first seven minutes.
The Italians drew first blood in the game after captain Lorenzo Cannone crashed over the Fijians' line and planted the ball across, despite Hughes' attempted tackle.
That came in the eighth minute, following a good break from halfback Stephen Varney, that sliced open the Fijian midfield, and fullback Tommaso Allan's conversion gave them an early 7-0 lead.
Fijian captain Tevita Ikanivere was penalised for playing ball on ground in the 12th minute and Allan extended the home team's lead to 10-0 from inside Fiji's 22 metre zone.
But Fiji came back hard and a lineout take inside the Italian's 22 metres saw Ikanivere dive over for their try. Flyhalf Ben Volavola converted, as Italy led 10-7.
Italy's defensive efforts after the 20th minute saw them stop three scoring opportunities from their visitors, managing three good turnovers as Fiji attacked.
A second Allan penalty in the 31st minute saw Fiji trailed their host 13-7 at halftime.
Fiji's Tevita Ikanivere leads an attack against Italy. Photo: Fiji Rugby Union
Fiji started the second half with a lot more determination, with prop Peni Ravai running on to a lineout win and driving his way through the Italian defence.

That saw Italy defending desperately on their line but they could not stop Ikanivere from diving over in between the posts in the 44th minute, with replacement flyhalf Caleb Muntz tipping the conversion over as Fiji claimed the lead 14-13.
That spurred Fiji into action with two consecutive bombs from Frank Lomani forcing errors in the Italian defence.
Taranaki Bulls reps Marika Parker in for his debut for Fiji, having played for Taranaki Bulls National Provincial Championship.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9e8: Watch: Boos in the arena after concert cancelled as emergency services attend scene
Thousands of people were evacuated from a concert in Manchester after an "unknown substance" was released into the crowd.

It happened towards the end of US rapper Don Toliver's show at the Co-op Live arena at about 22:00 GMT on Sunday, with music fans describing a "horrible smell" and people "screaming" and "coughing up blood".
One person was taken to hospital while more than 80 people were assessed for "eye and respiratory symptoms", the North West Ambulance Service said.
Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said a major incident was declared after reports of people suffering from the effects of an unknown substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas.
The force said 12,000 people had been evacuated and one fan told of "distressing scenes" with people "choking" and coughing as they left the venue.
Some fans have complained about security and a lack of searches going in to the concert.
The 22-year-old told BBC Radio Manchester : "I saw a lot of people streaming out and you go into this panic mode and you see a lot of people running out of the venue.
Joey Howe says he wondered if it was "part of the show" until the smell hit
He said it was like "time stopped in motion" when "there was nothing going on".
"We then decided to go out. People were coming through in wheelchairs choking - it was really distressing," Howe said.
"We then decided to leave the venue. It was just really distressing scenes and not something you want to see."
Howe also claimed security was "poor" and "very relaxed" with "people walking straight in".
Jessica Moult-Boffey, of Wigan, said people were "crying and screaming in pain" as they had fled the venue.
The 23-year-old told the BBC that she went to the exit and saw lads on the bridge which leads into Medlock Square "asking for help" but there were only two stewards outside.
She said she felt "confused on how something like that got into a venue of that size".
Concertgoers headed home after the performance was stopped by the incident
Malachi Clarke claimed security was "not good at all" at the venue.
The 19-year-old said: "They weren't checking bags, to the point where I had to ask them if they needed to check mine."
"Then we were told by a security guard it was chemical-related.
"After an hour or so of the gig being stopped, we were finally told to evacuate the venue."
Emergency services attended the Co-op Live arena in Manchester after a substance was let off in the crowd
Co-op Live said on its website there were a range of security measures, and while "some of these are visible, others you won't be able to see".
It said the arena used a "frictionless security screening that detects prohibited items without you needing to empty your pockets".

Harper, who was at the concert, told BBC Radio 5Live : "I was right on the opposite side and I was seeing people cough up blood - I mean, that's when it was really scary for some of us, especially my girlfriend and I.
"I was in shock because I had no idea what was going on because it just stopped and all the lights came on.
"I saw people getting wheelchairs out...I was fearful it was something even worse."
Forensic officers are at the arena carrying out investigations
Fans at the rapper's other gigs have claimed similar incidents have taken place earlier on his tour.
They reported that a spray or gas was released into the crowd in Zurich and Paris.
Entrances to Co-op Live remain cordoned off, with police officers and security stewards manning the perimeter which is taped off.
Crime scene investigators in white protective overalls have been moving in and out of the building, as work continues to establish the nature of the substance that caused the evacuation.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8e: The wife of disgraced comedian Russell Brand says she will "honour" the rules of his prison, a week after she read a message from her husband proclaiming his innocence.

Laura Brand, 39, drew criticism from ministers after reading out the message from inside HMP Littlehey last week, prompting the government to seek to have the episode removed from social media platforms.
She said on Sunday that she would continue to defend her family and herself over her portrayal in the media during the couple's weekly podcast, which she now presents alone.
Russell Brand, 51, is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
"Last week's episode drew a considerable amount of attention," Laura Brand said during this week's episode of Sunday Service.
"Now that I understand the parameters set by the brilliant and professional staff at HMP Littlehey, I will absolutely honour that."
In the relayed message last week, Russell Brand had said he was "not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for".
Laura Brand said she had spoken to him at the Cambridgeshire prison and said he was "OK".
Russell Brand was found guilty of raping a woman at his home in 2009, as well as three counts of sexual assault against three other women.
Further allegations have since been reported about him and some have called for consent laws to be revised .
His conviction has renewed conversation about safeguarding in the media industry, and whether some celebrities are still able to use their fame to prey on women and then silence them.
Ministers have pointed out that inmates are prohibited from making statements that are likely to cause their victims distress and have said Brand's message was being investigated.
A woman who alleges she was raped by Brand when she was 16, but who was not among the women whose accusations led to his conviction, said his prison message was "upsetting" and "really shocking" .

The government attempted to have the podcast removed from YouTube, but this was refused by its owner Google. Prime Minister Andy Burnham urged social media companies to "show some decency and take these videos down".

On Sunday, Laura Brand also said that Sunday Service would be a place where she would "continue to be proud to be a wife, a mother and a woman defending her family at a time when the media's image of what kind of a woman I am is under so much scrutiny".
She expressed feeling a mixture of "grief", "absence", "desolation" and "loneliness" since her husband's imprisonment.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3qj: Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum has died aged 83 after a long illness.
The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.

Known for his chaotic demeanour and trademark Stetson hat, he interviewed an array of stars from King Charles to Elton John, who described Meldrum as the "single most important influence in Australian pop music".
In a statement, Meldrum's family said he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.
"Affectionately dubbed 'the Guru', Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," the statement said.
Meldrum lived with an acquired brain injury after falling from a ladder in 2011.

Born in Victoria in 1943, he displayed a love of music from an early age and went on to host the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's music television programme Countdown, and later a segment on variety show Hey Hey, It's Saturday.
Meldrum in 2014 became the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) Hall of Fame.
Among his most famous interviews was a 1977 sit-down with King Charles, in which Meldrum could not calm his jitters.
He stumbled over his lines, declaring: "Your Royal Highness... Oh, oh, I'm sweating like a pig".

King Charles reflected on the infamous interview for Countdown's 40th anniversary special , saying: "There is an old showbusiness saying which warns never to work with animals or children. But nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum".
On Monday, Arts Minister Tony Burke said the country had lost an icon.

"One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music. A true champion of Australian talent, you will be missed, but never forgotten."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckp8: The Beatles famously performed on the rooftop of 3 Savile Row in January 1969

Plans to create a museum where The Beatles performed their last live performance is expected to be approved - but on condition no live music can be played on the rooftop that made the Mayfair venue famous.

Apple Corps Ltd, the company founded by the band, wants to convert 3 Savile Row into a seven-floor "cultural experience and exhibition" celebrating The Beatles, with a basement café-bar on the site of the studio where Let It Be was recorded in 1969.
The Beatles famously stunned locals in January 1969 by playing a set on the roof of the Grade II* listed building, which was Apple Corps' headquarters.
Westminster City councillors are due to vote on the plans on Tuesday.
The council papers set out for the first time the scale of the attraction Sir Paul McCartney announced in May .
Apple Corps is forecasting up to 900 visitors each weekday and 1,140 on weekends, entering in timed slots of 20 people every 10 minutes.
The basement café/bar would open until midnight seven nights a week, and events would be capped at 104 a year, averaging two events a week.
The draft conditions also state that no live music can be played on the terrace and any amplified music or speech should be noise limited. A two-metre-high acoustic barrier has also been proposed.
The location was the headquarters of The Beatles' record label, Apple Corps

The Savile Row Bespoke Association, which represents the street's bespoke tailors, has objected to the plans stating they are in conflict with the Savile Row Special Policy Area planning designation that aims to protect bespoke tailoring on the street.
It has also warned that narrow pavements "would lead to dangerous congestion and have a significant negative impact on those who visit and work on Savile Row".
The Mayfair Neighbourhood Forum has not objected in principle but said visitor numbers "need to be greatly reduced" and asked for the operation to be monitored for 12 months before any expansion.
Planning officers state "the proposal does not comply wholly" with the Special Policy Area but say the building's unique link to The Beatles justifies an exception.
They have suggested a clause that would require the building to revert to its previous office or retail use if the venue closed.
The infamous concert saw the Beatles play 10 songs before the police pulled the plug
Announcing the plans in May, Sir Paul told the BBC that tourists "come to England and they can go to Abbey Road, but they can't go inside" and described the Savile Row project as "a terrific idea".
He said visitors would "work your way up through the building… until you get to the top, where you go out on the roof and pretend to be a Beatle".
The Beatles at 3 Savile Row is due to open in 2027, if planning permission is obtained.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c32l: Cape Schanck, Victoria, dates from 1862 and depicts the dramatic coastline at the southernmost tip of Australia's Mornington Peninsula
A rediscovered 19th Century oil painting bought for £20 in a charity shop could be auctioned for up to £20,000.
Cape Schanck, Victoria, by Russian-Swiss artist Nicholas Chevalier, was discovered in a charity shop in Maidenhead, Berkshire.
It was brought to the attention of Adrian Biddell at London's Olympia Auctions, who established the painting was a Chevalier work that had been missing for 160 years.
"To find it now, quite unexpectedly, in a corner of the British high street, is an extraordinary find," he said.
The painting dates from 1862 and depicts the dramatic, rugged coastline at the southernmost tip of Australia's Mornington Peninsula, about 60 miles (96.5km) south of Melbourne.

The auction house said only two of five en plein air - meaning painted directly in front of the landscape it depicts - views of Cape Schanck by Chevalier that year were known to have survived until now.
Both are in the collection of the Art Gallery of New South Wales in Sydney.
It said the charity shop buyer had liked the landscape but had not been familiar with the artist or the painting's value.
Its appearance "resolves a longstanding gap in the documented history of Chevalier's work", it said.
It was leading Chevalier expert Simon Gregg who confirmed its whereabouts had previously been recorded as "unknown" in his catalogue of the artist's work.
"This was definitely painted en plein air," he said. "This was Chevalier's typical modus operandi."
Gregg added: "Most of the oil sketches have not survived, hence my delight that this one has shown up."
Biddell said Chevalier "was a remarkable visual talent, with an extraordinary ability to capture the drama, power and sheer scale of the natural world".
"The discovery of Cape Schanck, Victoria is hugely exciting," he said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c85y: Watch: Trailer for new programme detailing Princess Catherine's cancer journey
The Princess of Wales has spoken about how "cancer does change you," in a forthcoming documentary called Heal to be shown on the BBC.

"It changes your body, it changes you physically - but there is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you," says Catherine in the first glimpses from the documentary, which features her private thoughts on her illness and recovery.
The highly personal film, to be screened on BBC One on 29 November, will see Catherine share her experiences of cancer, saying: "Healing is a journey."
It includes new footage of her completing the Three Peaks Challenge earlier this year, which involved climbing the highest peaks in England, Scotland and Wales over a day.

"It's clear we're not meant to carry life's challenges alone," says Catherine's voice-over, accompanied by images of other cancer patients and the princess hugging her own family, including Prince William.
"It is often through pain that we realise there is a greater beauty that lies beyond that," she says, once again reflecting the sense of change from her cancer experience.
Kensington Palace shared a photo of Catherine doing the Three Peaks Challenge, ahead of the documentary
Catherine has never disclosed what type of cancer she faced, but in March 2024 she revealed that she had a diagnosis of cancer and was receiving chemotherapy .
In January 2025 she announced that she was in remission and in the following months began a gradual return to royal duties.
She has often spoken about her different understanding of life after her illness, and the need to take a more holistic approach to well-being beyond physical recovery.
The princess has talked about the good days and bad days that followed her treatment - and wanted to dispel the idea that patients could immediately return to how they felt before their illness.

This documentary, which will be introduced by Kirsty Young, promises to be the fullest and most personal account of that journey, with her own insights into the impact such illness can have and how she found her own healing process.

She has since returned to working for her charities and earlier this week was in India for the Earthshot Prize ceremony with Prince William, the first time they had travelled together on overseas royal duties since the princess's cancer treatment.
Catherine visited India for William's Earthshot Prize which was hosted in Mumbai - the first time she'd been at the Earthshot awards since 2022
Among the film crew for the documentary, as director of photography, was Will Warr, who has worked with Catherine and her family before.
His pictures have been used in a video birthday message by Catherine and a Christmas card which showed a relaxed image of the princess and Prince William and their children.
The filmmaker also made the personal video statement that marked the end of her chemotherapy in September 2024, with her message: "Out of darkness, can come light."

Kate Phillips, the BBC's chief content officer, said it was hoped the 30-minute documentary "will resonate with BBC viewers and provide comfort and support to those navigating their own health challenges".
Catherine was treated at The Royal Marsden Hospital and funds from the distribution of this documentary, which is to be broadcast in other countries, will be paid to The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity.
When cancer patients finish treatment at the London hospital they can symbolically ring a bell.
"I didn't ring the bell," says Catherine, speaking to her brother James Middleton.
"Maybe this is your ringing the bell," he says, about carrying out the Three Peaks Challenge and this documentary about her healing.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm3v: Peter Fluck alongside a satirical puppet of Margaret Thatcher that he created, pictured in 1992
Peter Fluck, co-creator of award-winning satirical puppet show Spitting Image, has died aged 85.
His family said he died in the early hours of Saturday at home in Cornwall, following a recent illness.

Spitting Image was immensely popular and sometimes controversial, running from 1984-1996 across 18 seasons, and featured puppet caricatures of celebrities, politicians and royals, including former Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother.
"The spirit that Spitting Image brought to the country was epoch defining," a family statement said.
"With Roger Law ('Luck and Flaw'), he brought a unique cutting edge to caricaturing that later evolved into a production company that created the TV series Spitting Image," it added.
"Peter's creative life continued after the series for many years from his studio in Cornwall. He was a private man who eschewed fame and attention."
The show won several awards, including one Bafta TV award and two Emmys and at its peak drew an audience of 15 million.
Fluck was born in Cambridge in 1941, and created the show alongside childhood friend Roger Law, who he met while studying at Cambridge School of Art.
Following school, both Fluck and Law moved to London and set up as freelance illustrators, and in 1976 set up their partnership 'Luck and Flaw' back in Cambridge.
"You could say we took the traditional newspaper editorial cartoon and put it on the screen," Fluck told ArtCornwall in an interview , external in 2006.
He described the show as being shown "at the difficult time of 10 o'clock on a Sunday night when all politicians should have been in bed".

Many of the characters included parodies of Thatcher's cabinet, with Douglas Hurd depicted with "Mr Whippy ice cream" hair, and her successor John Major caricatured as a dull, grey puppet with a penchant for peas.

"We did get quite a lot of approaches from politicians for their puppet to be made, because if you didn't appear as a puppet on Spitting Image you hadn't made it as a politician," Fluck said in an interview in 2011. , external
It was eventually axed by ITV because of declining audience numbers.

In a statement, the broadcaster said Fluck's "creative contribution to TV satire is simply unrivalled... his cutting edge puppetry and caricature skills, alongside the show's sharp and always shrewdly observed humour, became a defining part of the cultural zeitgeist.
"Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with his family and friends at this very sad time."
When he stepped away from the show, Fluck moved to Cornwall and focused his art on ceramics, printmaking and mobiles.
In 2018, Law donated his entire archive of Spitting Images to Cambridge University.
The collection - including original scripts, puppet moulds, drawings and recordings - was conserved and held in the library.
