Hundreds of New Zealand seeds grown in a simulated future atmosphere have been secured in a doomsday vault in the Arctic Circle.

The Svalbard Global Seed Vault safeguards more than 1.4 million seed samples from around the world. The vault, located in the mountain permafrost, stores copies of important seeds in a bid to preserve agricultural biodiversity and ensure there will be enough food in the future.
The latest shipment from the Margot Forde Genebank - based in Palmerston North and managed by the Bioeconomy Science Institute Maiangi Taiao - marked 10 years since New Zealand's first deposit.
According to Genebank director Kioumars Ghamkhar the 300 seed samples contained "vital genetic material".
This year, the deposit included seeds from grasses grown for more than 25 years in an enriched carbon dioxide atmosphere - "just in case disaster happens", he said.
Dr Ghamkhar with former Crop Trust executive director Marie Haga in 2016. The Crop Trust manages and funds the Svalbard.
Ghamkhar said the seeds could help develop future varieties capable of withstanding extreme climate shifts.
The climate-resilient varieties came about through natural change, rather than genetic modification, he said.
"When you impose some conditions on plants, they adapt and their genetics changes over time."
He said future deposits could include drought-resistant varieties that had adapted to growing in wetter conditions, for example.
While accepting that he and his small team played "an important role" Ghamkhar rejected the idea that New Zealand's future was in his hands.
So, how does the team choose what to send to the underground vault on a Norwegian archipelago?

"Basically, the criteria for us is what is important for New Zealand as its heritage, let's say, in agriculture. And then what is important for the world? And of course, climate change is nowadays an important factor."
The Genebank's long-term goal was to secure about 18,000 seed samples in the Arctic vault - about 10 percent of its entire collection.
Ghamkhar said the focus was on "backing up seed material" with economic and climate adaptive value, with ryegrass and white clover among the core species.
So far, the Genebank had shipped close to 3500 seed samples, dried and sealed inside double-layered aluminium pouches.
Ghamkar said visiting the Svalbard Global Seed Vault with the first deposit in 2016, was "unreal".
Everything from the "snow-covered land" in the height of summer and the long hours of daylight, "was just amazing," Ghamkhar said.
"The hotel I was staying at, the lady at the reception said that a week before there was a polar bear hitting the door trying to get in.
"So this is just fascinating and I think it was a privilege, really, to do that 10 years ago and one of my best experiences."
Ghamkhar said the seed vault, which has been up and running since 2008, was a realistic, rather than defeatist or pessimistic, project.
He said things disappeared and changed over time - sometimes due to human intervention, sometimes not.
"If they disappear and you don't collect and bring them in, you won't have any record of it. It's gone and it's gone forever.

"So if we have them [seeds] here, and also even better if we characterise them and get ready for the worst case scenario ... then it's a real thing that can affect our preparation and readiness for the future and survival of human beings."

Northland's first wind farm has been officially opened today as the region continues its transformation from energy importer to significant producer of renewable power.
Mercury's Kaiwaikawe Wind Farm, with 12 towers producing 77 megawatts (MW) of electricity in a good breeze, is not the biggest in the country by any means - but its turbines are by far the tallest .
Each measures 206m from ground to rotor tip, making them taller than any structure in New Zealand bar Auckland's Sky Tower.
The project, at Omamari, on the wild west coast north of Dargaville, cost $287 million.
The expected annual output of 220 gigawatt-hours (GWh) is roughly equivalent to the power used by 31,000 homes.
Mercury chief executive Stew Hamilton opened the wind farm this afternoon with Kaipara Deputy Mayor Gordon Lambert and Northland MP Grant McCallum.
Hamilton said the first turbines started generating power in July, with final commissioning, testing and site rehabilitation expected to continue until early 2027.
The project was on track to be completed on time and on budget.
Hamilton thanked mana whenua Te Roroa, landowner Pāmu and the Kaipara community for their support.
Getting the 80-metre-long turbine blades from Northport, on the east coast, to Dargaville and then up the west coast to Omamari was a major transportation feat.
About 180 people worked on site each day at the peak of construction. More than 250,000 hours of work had been clocked up without any serious accidents.
Kaiwaikawe boosted Mercury's generation diversity with wind farms in Northland, central North Island, Otago and Southland complementing the company's hydro and geothermal generation, Hamilton said.

"The wind blows differently across the country. Having wind farms spread across multiple regions reduces reliance on the weather in any one place, contributing to a more resilient and secure electricity system for New Zealand."
One of the objections raised when the wind farm was first mooted was its proximity to wetlands frequented by the endangered bittern or matuku-hūrepo.
The company had set up a $640,000 Bittern Management Fund to support DOC and iwi programmes protecting the birds, and made a $360,000 commitment to GPS tracking, Hamilton said.
The company was also contributing $30,000 a year to the Kaiwaikawe Community Fund.
The first two funding rounds had paid for, among other things, bikes for tamariki at Kaihu Valley School, science equipment for Dargaville Primary School and operating costs for Dargaville Menz Shed.

Just last month, Mercury opened the South Island's largest wind farm, the 46-turbine Kaiwera Downs near Gore . It cost just over $600 million, produced enough power for 96,000 homes, and was built in two stages.
Earlier this month the company broke ground on the $506m, 40-turbine Puke Kapo Hau Wind Farm in Otago .

Getting the enormous Kaiwaikawe turbine blades from Northport, on the opposite coast, to Omamari was a major transportation feat, with only one known mishap when a truck veered off a metal road into a drain.
Ngāwhā geothermal power station remains Northland's biggest producer of renewable energy.

The opening of Kaiwaikawe continues Northland's evolution from a power-importing region - reliant on electricity transported large distances over vulnerable transmission lines, as seen in the 2024 pylon collapse - to a significant producer of renewable energy.
The Far North is already a net exporter of energy, thanks to Top Energy's geothermal power plant at Ngāwhā , near Kaikohe, and Lodestone Energy's Kohirā Solar Farm just outside Kaitāia .

"We're at the point of making sure that we have all of the necessary contingency plans in place," he said.
"Low flows in the river itself are problematic, as would be changes in water conditions."

"There is a barge that Hamilton City Council invested in, which can be lowered into the river to allow us to take water from a deeper base than the fixed intake on the side of the river. That has never had to be used so we're hoping we can avoid that."

Winder said the water company has other demand management and water restriction plans that can be put in place.
This included working with the major water users, including Fonterra, Dairy Goat, coolstores and the council. Waikato Hospital's water supply is protected from any restrictions.
"Part of the plan is demand management across households as well as major users if that is necessary."
Winder said holiday hotspots could feel the impact of drought conditions due to the influx of visitors.
"Raglan's supplied by a spring, it has a finite capacity, demand can exceed supply we just need to be careful."

A report tabled with the IAWAI board this week sets out the wide-ranging readiness programme covers risk monitoring, demand management, operational contingency plans, communications, escalation and incident response.
The water company is working closely with both Hamilton City Council and Waikato District Council, as well as local Civil Defence and the Smart Water education programme.
The report notes another potential issue is water quality, such as algae blooms and natural arsenic levels which have increased in recent years during late spring and early summer.
"A water-quality event occurring at the same time as peak demand would create the most significant challenge because treatment output could reduce when demand is highest," the report said.
Monitoring plans are in place for the Waikato River and the IAWAI treatment plants.

Fonterra's application to dump up to 22 million litres of raw milk in Canterbury is "quite grim" when so many New Zealanders do not have enough to eat, says a poverty researcher.
While almost nine Olympic-sized swimming pools of raw milk could go down the drain, a third of people in some parts of the country are struggling to keep food on the table.

"The hunger monitor report from the New Zealand food network is showing that one in three families in the Waikato, which is a strong dairy producing region, don't have enough to eat and going hungry," poverty researcher Dr Rebekah Graham says.
"To hear that Fonterra, want to dump millions of perfectly fine milk simply to increase corporate profits is quite grim.

"I think it's a terrible indictment on our society, that we have normalised this and allowed this to happen, that somehow it's now acceptable for the largest company in terms of dairy, to just dump millions of litres of milk, because that's easier and cheaper for them, than actually considering how that milk might be used, to feed people, to nourish people."
Audio player for " Fonterra plans to dump 22 million litres of raw milk alarms experts " removed for printing

Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/environment/2751368%2Fit-s-going-to-waste-poverty-advocate-appalled-by-fonterra-s-plan-to-dump-millions-of-litres-of-raw-milk
She said while the proposal allowed for the dumping of 22 million litres of raw milk, for many even one litre was out of reach.
"If I was one of those families. struggling to pay $4 for a bottle of milk to then hear that it's all being poured out and going to waste. It would be heartbreaking."
Graham said the news reminded her of a woman she spoke to for her PHD on food insecurity, who was horrified that people tipped out their milk before heading on holiday.

"I thought of what it was like for her, who couldn't afford to feed her kids, but her milk was eked out. It was watered down. It was really valued. And I thought, imagine what that must be like, having to do that, and then hearing that this company's just simply doesn't care, and it's just going to throw it all away."
Environmental Law Initiative legal researcher Eliza Prestidge-Oldfield agreed. It has asked Environment Canterbury to reject the application.

"That's seven and a half thousand milk tankers full of milk. That's more milk than Fonterra has donated for the Kickstart Breakfast Programme in the 15 years that programme has been running. So you know, the quantities here I think are just staggering."
She said one of the ways Fonterra could dispose of the milk was by irrigating it to farmland.

"And so what we might end up seeing is something like bacterial changes in rivers, we might see algal blooms, we might see oxygen depletion, and also that soil the productivity of that soil is significantly affected, because it's having to sort of process this milk."
Prestidge-Oldfield said the dairy giant was trying to bypass scrutiny by the way it had applied for a variation of its existing wastewater discharge consents.
She said rejection would require Fonterra to apply for a new discharge consent.
The dairy giant said the move was necessary to manage a potential surplus caused by production constraints across the South Island.
Dairy sector commentator and Agri-Women's Development Trust general manager Julia Jones said it did not sound bad in perspective.

*Warning: This story contains details of assisted dying and may be upsetting for some readers
A family forced to take their elderly mother to Switzerland to fulfil her wish of assisted dying are calling for a law change so others do not have to go through the same ordeal.
Margaret Topzand, of Auckland, died in Zurich on 2 July. She was 93.
Justin Topzand said his mother had led a full and happy life, and was still in good health.
"There was nothing wrong with her. She was starting to show mild dementia and forgetfulness, but she was basically sick of living," he said.
"She felt that she'd done and seen everything and that it was time for her to go. And she wanted to go on her terms, without having to linger in a retirement home for years and years."
Margaret, a long-time supporter of voluntary euthanasia, called her sons together - Peter, Justin and Allister - to explain her wishes.
However, that request turned out to be far more difficult than anyone expected.
Margaret Topzand, seen here with son Peter, enjoying the sun during one of her last walks in the Swiss countryside.

The brothers discovered that New Zealand's End of Life Choice Act , which became law in 2021, only allowed assisted dying for people who had a terminal illness and were expected to die within six months.

"She had a few meetings with the three of us brothers, and said: 'Can't you help me?' And we realised we couldn't. Legally, we could not help her until Peter, my older brother, discovered that we could go to Switzerland with her."
What Peter Topzand had read in a newspaper article was that Swiss not-for-profit organisation Dignitas offered doctor-assisted suicide for foreign nationals - provided they met strict criteria.
Peter said his mother was still living independently, but finding that increasingly difficult.

Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/health/2751692%2Fshe-wanted-to-go-on-her-terms-auckland-mum-93-fulfils-wish-of-assisted-dying-in-zurich
Realising she needed a higher level of care, they visited a rest home to see if that would be a good option.

"There were all these old ladies in their wheelchairs, dribbling into their laps. It looked awful, even though it was a nice and expensive rest home, and mum said as we got in the car, 'I'm not doing it, I'm not going to be an old lady in a wheelchair, who doesn't know her own name, dribbling into her lap'. Her words were: 'Can't you help me to step out?'."
It was then that Peter mentioned, just as conversation, what he had read about in Switzerland.

"And she said, 'Well, let's do that, I want you to organise that', and I thought: 'shit'. I agonised over it a bit and spoke to my wife and to friends, and I came to the conclusion that while it was not my job to talk her out of it or prevent her from doing it, I wasn't prepared to be the one who actually orchestrated and facilitated my own mother's death. I just didn't want that."
Justin Topzand says his mother Margaret was a positive and inspirational woman who embraced life - and wanted the right to decide when to end it.
However, during his research, Peter had also stumbled onto the concept of death doulas, professionals who guide people through the process of dying.
It did not take long to find an end-of-life doula whose values meshed with their own.

A local resident says taxpayers could end up bearing the cost if a proposed mega housing development on flood-prone land in Christchurch goes ahead.

Tammy Wells is among residents who opposed the Whisper Creek development in north Christchurch, which would see 800 homes built across 170 hectares of land previously intended for a luxury gold course.
Wells said she was concerned the risks associated with the site could eventually become a financial burden on homeowners and taxpayers.
She questioned who who would be left responsible if the developer completed the project and walked away, leaving the council and the taxpayers to deal with the consequences.
The development attracted 63 submissions raising concerns about human health and natural hazards, including earthquake liquefaction and flooding from the nearby Styx River and heavy rainfall.
"If you suddenly then perhaps have 1600 cars all trying to evacuate out of two entrance exits at the one time, I mean, that just sort of spells disaster."
An independent commissioner who have given the project a green light found the risks could be adequately managed or mitigated.
Wells said she was not opposed to subdivisions but believed developments needed proper controls.
"I'm not anti-subdivision. I'm really not. But I think it's got to have controls and it doesn't feel like it does in this situation for us," she said.
Wells said the Council have got this wrong and that she is devastated by the decision.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/crime-and-jus: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/crime-and-justice/2750146%2Fyoung-soldier-admits-giving-cannabis-to-all-the-boys-at-burnham-military-camp
A soldier will be dismissed from the New Zealand Defence Force after admitting to supplying cannabis to other soldiers at Canterbury's Burnham Military camp.
Private Raniera Vercoe, 21, pleaded guilty to a total of six charges in connection with selling, supplying and using cannabis between September 2024 and June last year, at a court martial on Monday.
Vercoe was ordered to serve three months in detention at the Services Correctional Establishment at Burnham and will then be dismissed.

He was charged with selling and supplying cannabis to a soldier in November and December 2024, smoking cannabis at Burnham Military Camp and in Rotorua between September 2024 and June 2025, supplying cannabis to soldiers over the same period and possessing cannabis and a cannabis grinder in June 2025.
Vercoe also admitted consuming the class B drug MDMA at an unknown location in February 2025.
The court martial heard that cannabis was smelt coming from Vercoe's room in June last year.
During a search of his room by military police, cannabis, ziplock bags and a set of scales were found and his phone was seized.
The soldier was charged with smoking cannabis at Burnham Military Camp.
Cellphone analysis showed a series of message referring to supplying and using cannabis.
The summary of facts said text messages showed that Vercoe supplied at least one ounce, or 28 grams, of cannabis between September 2024 and June 2025.
The messages outlined selling small amounts of cannabis on three occasions and discussed smoking cannabis.
In a statement to military police, Vercoe admitted that various slang terms referred to cannabis.
He said he did not sell cannabis but "would give it to all the boys" and people would put money in his bank account without his knowledge.
Vercoe said a person would at times offer to buy him dinner in exchange for cannabis or "cones" he had shared with him.
In a December 2024 text message a soldier inquired about getting cannabis on "tick", or asked if he was sold out.
In another text message in April 2025, Vercoe offered to supply cannabis to a solider and said he was going to "wake and bake", suggesting he was planning to smoke cannabis.
Defence lawyer Josh Lucas said that Vercoe's sentence should reflect his youth at the time of the offending.
He said Vercoe was also now a father of two and the main breadwinner for his family.
Lucas said that Vercoe had counselling relating to the offending and was drug-free.
In sentencing, Judge Jonathan Moses said using and dealing drugs within a military environment was dangerous and an extremely serious breach of standards.
He said Vercoe's commander should be able to rely on him and others not to be under the influence of drugs, especially given the use of weapons and vehicles.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te-manu-korih: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/te-ao-maori/2751791%2Fnational-iwi-chairs-forum-meets-in-wellington
Iwi leaders have gathered in Wellington this week for a meeting of the National Iwi Chairs Forum.
More than 200 iwi delegates were welcomed to Waiwhetū marae in Lower Hutt on Monday.
It is the Forum's last meeting for the year, the next will be at Waitangi in February 2027.
Deputy Chairperson of Te Rūnanga o Te Āti Awa Karepa Wall told RNZ this weeks hui will focus on three pou, or pillars.
First how to capitalise on iwi partnerships around the globe for the benefit of iwi members, second what does mātauranga look like when Māori set the rules and define success.
And thirdly the environment, a discussion which Wall said will involve making room for the next generation of iwi leaders.

"Our big tōtara that are here today they were planted 100 years ago by our tūpuna. We've got to think like that and we've got to plant some tōtara today so that our mokopuna in 100 years time when we're not here can also take shelter under that tree."
Bringing rangatahi into the fold has been part of the Forum, which has its own Ngā Rangatahi ā Iwi leaders group, for a long time, he said.

"We're pushing that a little bit further today to make sure that actually we're not just letting them in the room to have a listen and we're not just letting them in here to see how things go. We're actually letting them determine what those things are that we need to be as well.

"Our rangatahi can't do their work if we don't give them pūtea to do the mahi. They can't do their work if we don't get off the paepae and let them sit with us. We can't let them come along and just have listening ears on they actually have to have a voice as well."
Te Rūnanga o Ngāi Tahu Kaiwhakahaere (Chair) Justin Tipa said iwi leaders need to be deliberate about succession planning.
"It's just about how do we develop the programmes and create the opportunities to bring those young ones through and give them meaningful governance learning opportunities."
Wall said the Forum made a deliberate decision not to invite politicians to this weeks hui

"The deliberate decision not to have politicians is merely because the conversations or discussions that we want to have is about Māori setting up what actually the pathway is for Māori and so we don't need politicians to do that today.
"That doesn't mean that they can't participate in a forum but it's just at the moment our goal is for Māori to be able to really reach for the stars and see what we can do."
Tipa said no doubt there will still be some discussion during the hui about what the new government may hold for Māori.
"Our hope is that whatever the colour of government, that there's a meaningful relationship and a meaningful desire to work with iwi for the betterment of all New Zealanders, I think.

"We saw from some of the outgoing ministers of the last government some of the regrets and some of the thoughts that they shared around that, so I'm hopeful that while we've seen some benefits and some focus on things like investment and infrastructure, we can't forget about the well-being of our people who are absolutely feeling the pinch of the cost of living and everything else at the moment."

Following the pōwhiri three prominent Māori leaders received Te Whare Pukenga Awards, Sir Mason Durie (Rangitāne, Ngāti Kauwhata, Ngāti Raukawa) an academic widely recognised for his pioneering work in Māori health, Dame Pania Tyson-Nathan (Rongomaiwahine, Ngāti Kahungunu) the CEO of New Zealand Māori Tourism and Dr Te Taku Parai (Ngāti Toa Rangatira) a longstanding advocate for Māori development in Porirua.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/community/275: Hamilton's giant Christmas tree is heading for its last hurrah this festive season unless someone steps up to foot the bill for a replacement.
The 27-metre tree, which is going up right now in Garden Place, is one of the country's tallest and takes about two weeks to put together.

But the steel frame that supports the tree has been welded up so many times since its first outing in 2011 that experts advise it is not safe to do so anymore, Jesse Gibbeson from Hamilton's Christmas Charitable Trust told Checkpoint.
And the cheapest quote to replace it has come in at $220,000 to $250,000, Gibbeson said.

"The joints and the parts that are holding it together, they've been welded so many times that it's gotten to the point where they can't be welded safely again and… we want it to be standing up for a whole month and not to fall down."
Audio player for " Hamilton Christmas tree to be retired after 15 years " removed for printing
A Hamilton Christmas without the tree just would not be the same, he said.

"With our tree-lighting festival due to go on this Saturday night, we're expecting a good 5000 to 6000 people, or probably more, in Garden Place to watch [it] light up. It's a huge festival and it's quite a big highlight for Hamilton.
"Once it's up, it lights up from 9 o'clock every night. It's got a brand-new light display.
"We've got lots of different images displayed on our tree, from Santa to the Christmas Trust jingles.
"We've got the reindeer, all the different Christmas objects as well as different light shows."
Could Hamilton not make do with a big pine tree? "Well, we could. I don't think it would be the same as our Christmas tree we've had for all these years," Gibbeson said.
The only salvation would be if someone came forward with a better price, as the Christmas Charitable Trust relied on grants and lottery funds to keep running the event.
"We work really hard every year to apply for funds and grants and every effort to keep Christmas going in Hamilton," he said.
"If anyone can do a cheaper deal for us and make Christmas happen in Hamilton again every year, I think Hamilton and Waikato would be very grateful."

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/business/2751: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/business/2751723%2Fegg-producers-to-eggsplain-colony-and-cage-connection-more-clearly-on-labels
Animal welfare group SAFE is claiming victory after its complaint about misleading egg labels prompted some big producers to change their branding.

SAFE filed a complaint to the Commerce Commission in 2025, saying that the industry was failing to make it clear that colony-laid eggs were laid in cages, and this was a breach of the Fair Trading Act.

It alleged that using the words 'colony' or 'colony-laid' and not 'caged' gave shoppers the wrong impression about how the eggs are produced and masked the fact the layer hens actually lived in cages.
Audio player for " Egg producers change labels after complaints they are misleading " removed for printing

Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/business/2751723%2Fegg-producers-to-eggsplain-colony-and-cage-connection-more-clearly-on-labels
Although battery-caged hens have been banned since 2022, colony cages - which are much larger but house dozens of hens - are still allowed.
A 2024 verian poll found 41 percent of people surveyed thought that 'colony laid' meant the hens lived in barns and were free to roam outside.
Only 16 percent realised it meant the eggs came from caged hens.
The Commerce Commission has now informed egg producers that it thought the labels could be a breach of the Fair Trading Act, which SAFE said has prompted changes.
SAFE head of campaigns Jessica Chambers told Checkpoint that three brands had committed to changing their labelling.
Morning Harvest, Farmer Brown and Sure As Eggs had all confirmed they would be putting the word 'cage' next to the word 'colony' on their packaging.
Chambers said the addition of the word would allow people to make informed decisions about the eggs they were buying.
"We're a compassionate nation and I think if we have this knowledge and we know what we're actually being sold, people will probably not choose the caged products.

"The lives of these animals is being hidden from the public for a very specific reason, and that's because the majority of New Zealanders don't support intensive factory farming of animals and keeping hens in cages for the entirety of their lives"
Chambers said SAFE was concerned that many New Zealanders thought that hens were no longer being found in cages.
"Colonies are very sanitized word to use to describe these systems."
Battery hen cages could hold about six hens, and were barren with nothing in them except wire, but Chambers said colony cages were not much of an improvement.
"You can have up to 80 birds in one cage, and the law allows hens to be given space roughly the size of an A4 sheet of paper to live in for the duration of their lives - they never step outside."
There are currently no legal requirements for any animal product distributors to disclose the conditions the animals they are farming live in.
Chambers said there should be an obligation for companies to do so.
"I think the more information New Zealanders have to choose where they're spending their hard-earned money, the better."
The Egg Producers Federation of New Zealand said members have been told that using the word colony on its own risks breaching the Fair Trading Act.
Its advice was to either add the word 'cage' alongside 'colony', or remove the term 'colony' altogether, so there's no reference to the housing method.
The federation said it could not comment on what individual producers were doing, but said they was aware of their responsibility to comply.

Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/education/2750839%2Fpay-equity-law-changes-exert-a-dystopian-effect-over-low-paid-women-says-union-for-teacher-aides
The union for teacher aides say it is "shocking" the Government has barred pay equity reviews for 10 years, claiming last year's law changes exert a "dystopian" effect over low-paid women.
But Ministry of Education lawyers say the amended law is explicit in setting a 10-year bar to review claims, and the union cannot circumvent it.

NZEI Te Riu Roa brought a case to the Employment Court in Wellington on Monday , arguing the Ministry of Education had an obligation to ensure pay equity, including recurring reviews of previous settlements, despite the 2025 changes.

Teacher aides had a 2020 pay equity settlement - which included a three-yearly review - and union members rallied outside court on Monday, saying their pay rates in real terms had dropped in the six years' since the settlement.

Megan Vant, the lawyer for the Secretary of Education, said a specific section of the 2025 amendment limits new pay equity claims for the same group to every 10 years, apart from exceptional circumstances.

Vant referred to Minister Brooke van Velden's statements in the House that short review periods made it difficult to decide whether pay differences were due to pay equity issues re-emerging, or short-term labour market issues.
"She described the ability to raise a claim again after 10 years as having a 10-year review date, and as more robust."
She also said claims required a lot of data gathering, analysis and resources for both parties, and the 10-year limit sought to address that.
While employers still had an obligation for pay equity, it was not an ongoing responsibility to update pay equity pay rates during those 10 years, Vant said.

Susan Hornsby-Geluk, co-lawyer for the Secretary of Education, said she wanted to address the "elephant in the room" of last week's High Court judgement, which found the Government breached women's rights when it scrapped dozens of pay equity claims last year .
Despite the ruling, the Employment Court still needed to apply the current law and the intention behind it, she said.
She said Justice Paul Radich's judgement confirmed no reviews could occur in a 10-year period.
"Rightly or wrongly, what the act does is for a period of 10 years is removes protections against re-emerging discrimination."
Ally Kingi at the teacher aide pay equity rally outside the Wellington District Court.
Lawyer for NZEI Peter Cranney said he felt uncomfortable arguing this case with a caretaker Government in charge.

"Here we have the Government coming into the court a few days after finding that Parliament unlawfully breached the Bill of Rights Act, and urging the Court, despite the caretaker nature of the arrangements currently in place, to take the most chilling and narrow view to this issue."
Employers still had an obligation to ensure pay equity due to another section in the Act setting out employer responsibilities, he said.
"The language of that section says [the Secretary of Education] does have [an obligation]."
The law applied to tens or hundreds of thousands of low-paid women, and in a "shocking result", prevented workers from bargaining about pay equity issues for at least 10 years, he said.
https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/rotorua-r: Rotorua runner Hannah Gapes has won the NCAA Division I women’s cross country championship in Terre Haute, Indiana, in the United States, and set a course record.
The NCAA runs university sport in the United States, and Division I is its top level. Cross country is running over grass, dirt and hills rather than on a track.

Gapes, who runs for North Carolina State University (NC State), finished the 6km course in 18 minutes 44.3 seconds on 21 November 2026 (US time). She crossed the line more than seven seconds ahead of second place, Salma Elbadra from South Carolina.
She is only the second New Zealander to win the women’s title. The first was Kim Smith, who won on the same course 22 years ago.
It was Gapes’ last ever NCAA cross country race, and it finished off an unbeaten season. She took 13 seconds off the course record she set there in October.
Gapes was also New Zealand’s women’s senior cross country champion in 2025.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/niue-ocea: A project protecting the ocean around the small Pacific nation of Niue has won one of the world’s most prestigious environmental prizes.

The Niue Ocean Wide Trust took out the Revive Our Oceans category at the Earthshot Prize, awarded at a ceremony in Mumbai, India. Nearly 7000 projects from 169 countries entered this year, so winning is a huge achievement.
Prince William and Princess Catherine attended the ceremony, along with former New Zealand Prime Minister Dame Jacinda Ardern and Niue’s Prime Minister, Dalton Tagelagi.

The prize is worth millions of dollars. The trust works in partnership with the Niue Government, and people and groups around the world can already sponsor the protection of one square kilometre of Niue’s ocean for NZ$250 each.

The money raised so far has helped fund coastal protection projects in local villages, paid for insurance in case of climate disasters like cyclones, and even helped pay for half of Niue’s high school students to learn how to scuba dive.
In a Facebook post, the trust said the win belonged to the people of Niue.
Niue is aiming to raise $32 million in total to protect and manage its huge ocean area. Winning the Earthshot Prize has now pushed them over the halfway mark towards that goal.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/scientist: For the first time ever, scientists might have directly watched one star swallow up a smaller star right next to it, in a galaxy far, far away.
The giant star, nicknamed “Bao,” is a red giant about 2.5 million light-years away in the Andromeda galaxy. It is seven times heavier than our sun, and a huge 350 times wider.

Scientists first noticed the star getting brighter back in 2018. By 2023, using special telescopes in the United States, they could see it was definitely growing more luminous. Then, near the end of 2025, they spotted a massive eruption of light coming from the star.

NASA’s powerful James Webb Space Telescope studied the star just 47 days after that eruption, giving scientists important clues. They believe a smaller companion star, about 70 percent as heavy as our sun, spiralled into the giant star’s centre, causing a huge explosion.
“Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult,” said lead scientist Viraj Karambelkar, from Columbia University in the United States.
“When a star engulfs its companion, its effect is very subtle, like throwing a bucket of water in a large ocean,” he said. “I was absolutely flabbergasted when we saw this.”
Karambelkar said the discovery proves something scientists had only guessed at before. “I can’t wait to find more,” he said.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/historic-: A carved Māori meeting house that sheltered 50 people during a volcanic eruption almost 140 years ago is finally coming home to Rotorua.
The wharenui (meeting house) is called Hinemihi. She sheltered dozens of people when Mt Tarawera erupted in 1886, one of New Zealand’s most powerful eruptions.

Six years after the eruption, the departing British Governor, William Hillier Onslow, bought Hinemihi and shipped her all the way to his family home in the United Kingdom. She has stood there ever since.

Now, after years of asking, Ngāti Hinemihi will finally get their wharenui back. Officials from the UK’s National Trust and British Council met with Heritage New Zealand and Ngāti Hinemihi in Auckland this week to plan the journey home.
“As long as you’ve got that whare, as long as you’ve got Hinemihi, you’ve got us as well, because we belong to that house,” said Jim Schuster, of Ngāti Hinemihi.
The National Trust has confirmed Hinemihi will be back by 2028, although it still isn’t decided whether she will travel home by air or by sea.
“It is taking a long time, but it’s right to do it well and do it properly,” said Natasha Woollard, of the National Trust.
To thank the UK for looking after Hinemihi so well, Ngāti Hinemihi are gifting new carvings, carrying on the work of her original carver, Tene Waitere.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/all-black: The All Blacks have suffered their biggest-ever defeat to a northern hemisphere team, going down 37-12 to England at Twickenham in London.
It was a tough day for coach Dave Rennie’s side, who had also lost to Wales in Cardiff the week before.
England raced into an early lead when Henry Slade scored just five minutes in, after a clever kick from team-mate Fin Smith.
The home side kept piling on the pressure, holding the ball for long periods and scoring further tries through Jack van Poortvliet and number eight Ben Earl.
The All Blacks fought back before halftime, with prop Ethan de Groot helping set up a try to keep them within reach.
But errors and missed tackles let England pull away in the second half, with flanker Ollie Chessum scoring in the corner.
The All Blacks’ best moment came when a slick offload set up a try for veteran Beauden Barrett, who was playing his 150th test for New Zealand.
England added two more scores late in the game to seal the 37-12 win, handing the All Blacks their fifth loss of the season.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/voyager-1: NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft has become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth. It passed the milestone on 18 November 2026.

A light-day is how far light travels in a whole day. Voyager 1 is now about 26 billion kilometres away, more than four times as far as Pluto is from the Sun. That means a signal sent from Earth takes 24 hours to reach the spacecraft.

Voyager 1 is about the size of a small car and launched from Florida, in the United States, on 5 September 1977. Along the way, it photographed Jupiter, Saturn and Titan, which is Saturn’s largest moon.

In 1990, it took 64 pictures that together made the first “family portrait” of the solar system. In 2012, it moved beyond the reach of the Sun’s magnetic field and into interstellar space, which is the space between stars.
The spacecraft has lasted far longer than anyone expected, but eight of its 10 science instruments no longer work. Within the next ten years, scientists may receive its very last signal.
For now, Voyager 1 is still sending back information about space beyond our solar system. Next year, it and its twin, Voyager 2, will both have been in space for 50 years.
Pānui: Kua tae a Voyager 1 ki te tawhiti o te light-day kotahi i Papatūānuku
Ko te waka ātea a NASA, a Voyager 1, te mea tuatahi i hangaia e te tangata kua tae ki te tawhiti o te light-day kotahi i Papatūānuku. I tae atu ia ki taua tohu i te 18 o Noema 2026.

Ko te light-day te tawhiti e haere ai te marama i te roanga o te rā katoa. Kei te tata ki te 26 piriona kiromita te tawhiti o Voyager 1 i tēnei wā, neke atu i te whā whakareatanga o te tawhiti o Pluto i te Rā. Nō reira, e 24 hāora te roa kia tae atu tētahi tohu i tukuna mai i Papatūānuku ki te waka ātea.

He rite te rahi o Voyager 1 ki tētahi motukā iti, ā, i whakarewaina mai i Florida, i Amerika, i te 5 o Hepetema 1977. I tōna haerenga, i tango whakaahua ia o Hupita, o Hatana, me Titan, te marama nui rawa o Hatana.

I te tau 1990, i tango ia i ngā whakaahua e 64, ā, i hanga ngātahi ai te “whakaahua whānau” tuatahi o te pūnaha o te Rā. I te tau 2012, i haere ia ki tua atu o te papa autō o te Rā, ki te ātea i waenganui i ngā whetū.

Kua roa ake te ora o te waka ātea i tā te katoa i whakaaro ai, engari kua kore e mahi ngā taputapu pūtaiao e waru o ōna taputapu e 10. I roto i ngā tau tekau e heke mai nei, tērā pea ka whiwhi ngā kaipūtaiao i tōna tohu whakamutunga rawa.
I tēnei wā, kei te tuku mai tonu a Voyager 1 i ngā mōhiohio mō te ātea i tua atu o tō tātou pūnaha o te Rā. Ā tērā tau, ka 50 tau a ia me tōna māhanga, a Voyager 2, e noho ana i te ātea.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/leaders-o: US President Donald Trump, China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin are holding their first-ever three-way meeting. The talks are taking place on 19 November 2026 in Shenzhen, China.
The meeting is happening alongside Apec, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. Apec is a big gathering of countries in the region that meet to talk about trade.
No one knows exactly what the leaders will discuss in private, but there are some big issues affecting all three countries.
The war between the US and Israel on one side and Iran on the other has hurt economies around the world. China is the biggest buyer of Iran’s oil.
The US and China are also racing to become the world leader in artificial intelligence, or AI.

Russia has been more cut off from other countries since it invaded Ukraine in 2022. Experts think a breakthrough on ending that war is unlikely. European leaders, and especially Ukraine, are worried about talks that don’t include anyone from Ukraine.

Vladimir Putin has led Russia since 1999, sometimes as President and sometimes as Prime Minister. Donald Trump began his second term as US President in 2025, after first serving from 2017 to 2021. Xi Jinping has been China’s leader since 2012.
BBC China Correspondent Laura Bicker said the meeting is a chance for President Xi to show China as a bridge between big countries.
Details of what the three leaders agree on, if anything, are expected once the talks are over.
Pānui: Ka hui ngā kaiārahi o Amerika, Haina me Rūhia mō te wā tuatahi

Kei te hui tahi te Perehitini o Amerika, a Donald Trump, te Perehitini o Haina, a Xi Jinping, me te Perehitini o Rūhia, a Vladimir Putin, mō te wā tuatahi rawa. Kei te tū te hui i te 19 o Noema 2026 ki Shenzhen, i Haina.
Kei te tū te hui i te taha o Apec, arā, te Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. He hui nui a Apec mā ngā whenua o tēnei rohe hei kōrero mō te hokohoko.
Kāore tētahi e mōhio pū ki ngā kōrero a ngā kaiārahi i tā rātou hui tūmataiti, engari he take nui kei te pā ki ngā whenua e toru.
Kua raru ngā ōhanga huri noa i te ao i te pakanga i waenganui i Amerika me Iharaira i tētahi taha, me Iran i tērā taha. Ko Haina te kaihoko nui rawa o te hinu o Iran.
Kei te whakataetae hoki a Amerika rāua ko Haina kia noho ko rātou te kaiārahi o te ao mō te atamai hangahanga, arā, te AI.

Kua noho mokemoke ake a Rūhia i ētahi atu whenua mai i tana whakaeke i Ūkareina i te tau 2022. E whakaaro ana ngā tohunga kāore pea e kitea he huarahi hou hei whakamutu i taua pakanga. Kei te māharahara ngā kaiārahi o Ūropi, otirā a Ūkareina, mō ngā hui kāore he tangata nō Ūkareina e uru ana.

Kua ārahi a Vladimir Putin i a Rūhia mai i te tau 1999, i ētahi wā hei Perehitini, i ētahi wā hei Pirimia. I tīmata a Donald Trump i tana wāhanga tuarua hei Perehitini o Amerika i te tau 2025, i muri i tana wāhanga tuatahi mai i te tau 2017 ki te tau 2021. Ko Xi Jinping te kaiārahi o Haina mai i te tau 2012.
E ai ki te kaikawe kōrero o te BBC i Haina, a Laura Bicker, he whai wāhitanga tēnei hui mā te Perehitini Xi ki te whakaatu i a Haina hei arawhiti i waenganui i ngā whenua nunui.
Ā muri i te hui, ka mōhiotia ngā mea i whakaaetia e ngā kaiārahi e toru, mēnā he mea i whakaaetia.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/study-fin: If your cat keeps meowing at you, it might be asking for a hand. A new study from the University of São Paulo in Brazil has found that cats use meows, along with eye contact, to ask their owners for help.

The researchers visited 38 cats in their own homes. Each cat was given a treat trapped inside a small plastic box with holes in it, so it could see and smell the snack but couldn’t get it out by itself.

When a person was in the room, the cats meowed 85 times, compared with just 20 times when they were alone. That’s about four times as many. Overall, the cats were 16 times more likely to meow when a human was around.

With no person nearby, the cats mostly stayed quiet, stood still and stared at the door. When a person was there, the cats meowed while looking straight at them, and kept glancing back and forth between the human and the box.
The researchers also found that feral cats meow much less than pet cats. Feral cats live on their own and don’t belong to anyone.
The study was published in the journal Animal Behaviour . It says meowing isn’t just a cat showing how it feels. It plays a “communicative role”, which means it’s a way for cats to talk to people.
So next time your cat meows and stares at you, it may simply be asking for a little help.

Mēnā ka miau tonu tō ngeru ki a koe, tērā pea kei te tono āwhina ia. Kua kitea e tētahi rangahau hou nā te University of São Paulo i Parīhi, ka miau ngā ngeru, ka titiro hoki ki ngā kanohi, hei tono āwhina i ō rātou rangatira.

I toro atu ngā kairangahau ki ngā ngeru e 38 i ō rātou ake kāinga. I hoatu he kai reka ki ia ngeru, kua mau i roto i tētahi pouaka kirihou iti he kōputaputa ōna. Ka kite, ka hongi te ngeru i te kai, engari kāore e taea e ia anake te tango mai.

I te wā he tangata i roto i te rūma, e 85 ngā miau a ngā ngeru, engari e 20 noa iho i te wā i a rātou anake. Tata ki te whā whakareatanga te nui ake. Ina whakarāpopotohia, e 16 whakareatanga te nui ake o te tūponotanga ka miau ngā ngeru mēnā he tangata kei reira.

Ki te kore he tangata i te taha, i noho wahangū te nuinga o ngā ngeru, i tū mārie, ā, i titiro atu ki te kūaha. I te wā he tangata kei reira, i miau ngā ngeru me te titiro tika atu ki taua tangata, ā, i huri haere tō rātou titiro i waenganui i te tangata me te pouaka.
I kitea anō e ngā kairangahau he iti ake te miau a ngā ngeru mohoao i tō ngā ngeru mōkai. Ka noho motuhake ngā ngeru mohoao, ehara i te mōkai a tētahi.

I tāngia te rangahau ki te hautaka Animal Behaviour . E ai ki te rangahau, ehara te miau i te whakaatu noa a te ngeru i ōna kare-ā-roto. He “tūranga whakawhitiwhiti kōrero” tōna, arā, he huarahi mā ngā ngeru hei kōrero ki te tangata.
Nō reira, ā muri ake nei, ina miau tō ngeru me te titiro mai ki a koe, tērā pea kei te tono āwhina noa iho ia.
